result.title: The Consumption Layer Should Generate Itself
result.thesis: Hand-building star schemas one business question at a time is a hidden tax: it produces a drifting galaxy of inconsistent marts, fan traps, and "which fact table" confusion. Because the business layer (DAB) already declares entities, keys, relationships, grain, measures and history, everything the consumption layer needs is already known — so the consumption layer (DAR) should be generated from it, not typed out. The concrete generated shape is Francesco Puppini's Unified Star Schema: a single event-based "bridge" (super fact) built by walking the business model graph along many-to-one edges only, which makes measures additive by construction and yields an explicit sliceability contract. Every other consumption format — data mart, OBT, classic star, feature table — is then a projection/selection of the same model rather than a separate build.

mandates.claim: Star schemas belong in the consumption layer (DAR, Data According to Requirements: the layer shaped to what the consumer needs), not in the business layer — this post is 'the other half of that argument' about what DAR should be and where it comes from.
mandates.implication: DAR is the only layer allowed to contain star/USS/OBT/mart shapes; DAB must stay free of them.

mandates.claim: The consumption layer should generate itself from the business model rather than being built by hand, one question at a time. 'The question is not which star schema to build by hand. The question is why we are building them by hand at all.'
mandates.implication: DAR must be a code-generation target driven by the DAB model; no hand-authored consumption SQL as the primary path.

mandates.claim: The generated USS is a single table, the bridge, that connects every entity to every other entity it can legitimately reach. Puppini suggested calling it a 'super fact' rather than a bridge, to break free of what 'bridge' means in the Kimball world. It holds all the relations and all the measures in one place.
mandates.implication: Generate one central bridge table holding all relations and all measures — not per-subject-area facts.

mandates.claim: In a USS you stop sorting tables into facts and dimensions. Every entity can play both roles — an order is a thing you measure and a thing you slice by, so is a customer, so is a product.
mandates.implication: The generator must not classify model entities as fact vs dimension; each entity gets both measure and slicing treatment.

mandates.claim: No fan traps, because the bridge is built to never fan out. No 'which fact table', because there is one.
mandates.implication: Fan-out safety is a build-time invariant of the generator, not a query-time discipline for analysts.

mandates.claim: The bridge must be event-based: instead of one row per entity instance, one row per measurement event, each carrying its own date. An order placed sets the date to the order date, an order shipped sets it to the shipped date, an order due sets it to the required date. This is what earns the 'answers almost everything' claim.
mandates.implication: Bridge grain = measurement event, with a per-event date column so every measure across every process lands on one canonical calendar; 'what happened in Q1' spans orders, shipments and returns on a single timeline without stitching star schemas.

mandates.claim: The generator walks the business model as a graph. For each entity, it follows the relationships that go from many to one and inherits the keys and measures of everything it reaches. 'The rule is short: follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it.'
mandates.implication: Implement bridge construction as an n:1-only graph traversal with key/measure inheritance along each safe path (order line -> order -> customer means the order line inherits both).

mandates.claim: A many-to-one step is safe because many order lines rolling up to one order cannot double-count the order. A many-to-many step has no safe direction at all, so the generator skips it and tells you.
mandates.implication: The generator must detect m:n edges, exclude them from the walk, and emit a warning naming the skipped edge — silent omission is not acceptable.

mandates.claim: What you are left with, for every entity, is the exact set of dimensions its measures are additive along. 'Not additive if you remember to be careful. Additive by construction, with the safe paths worked out for you.'
mandates.implication: Additivity is derived and guaranteed by the traversal, and must be materialized as an artifact, not left as tribal knowledge.

mandates.claim: The model is self-describing: the same model that builds the bridge also knows, for every measure and every dimension, whether you can slice that measure by that dimension, and how. That is a sliceability contract.
mandates.implication: Generation must emit a measure x dimension sliceability matrix alongside the bridge tables.

mandates.claim: The sliceability contract 'doesn't have to live in a proprietary corner. Express it as a vendor-neutral semantic contract (e.g. OSI) and any BI tool or AI agent can read it directly.'
mandates.implication: Publish the contract in an open/vendor-neutral semantic format so BI tools and agents consume it directly; do not lock it into a vendor semantic layer.

mandates.claim: Because the list of sliceable combinations is explicit, you can read off exactly which questions the model answers and which it does not, before you trust it with anything. 'Coverage is not a matter of faith.'
mandates.implication: Coverage must be inspectable as a pre-trust artifact — the contract doubles as the coverage report.

mandates.claim: This does not replace your BI tool, it feeds it. You point Power BI, Tableau, or Qlik at the bridge, or build your semantic model on top of it, instead of hand-building a star for every report.
mandates.implication: The bridge is the BI integration surface; no per-report star building downstream.

mandates.claim: Excel must not be skipped — 'A single bridge is a PivotTable's best friend.' Point Excel at the bridge and an analyst can slice the whole model, on one calendar, without waiting on anyone.
mandates.implication: The bridge's physical shape must be directly PivotTable-consumable (single wide table, one calendar), not just API/semantic-layer accessible.

mandates.claim: Once the business is modeled you have not committed to one consumption format. USS, data mart, One Big Table, classic star, and feature table are all projections of the same model — 'not things you build, things you select.'
mandates.implication: Build a projection mechanism over one model rather than separate pipelines per shape; a finance mart is a selection of finance entities, not a separate build.

mandates.claim: One Big Table 'can be generated flat, from the model or from the USS.'
mandates.implication: Two valid generation sources for OBT; the builder picks one.

mandates.claim: Everything a consumption model needs is already declared in a proper business layer — DAB is 'the layer where you model entities, keys, relationships, and history the way the business actually sees them'; the grain, the relationships and the measures are all sitting right there.
mandates.implication: DAB must explicitly declare entities, keys, relationships, history, grain and measures — the generator has no other input to read.

mandates.claim: Relationship direction and cardinality are load-bearing: the generator distinguishes n:1 (safe), 1:n (fan-out) and m:n (no safe direction).
mandates.implication: Cardinality must be a first-class, explicitly declared property of every relationship in the DAB model.

mandates.claim: 'The USS doesn't model your business for you.' The hard work moves to defining your entities, your keys, and your relationships once, properly. 'Get that layer right and everything downstream generates. Get it wrong and the generated USS will faithfully reproduce the mess.'
mandates.implication: DAB modeling quality is the prerequisite risk; invest review/testing effort there rather than in DAR.

mandates.claim: If your domain leans hard on many-to-many, you will model around it, and that is real work.
mandates.implication: Budget explicit DAB remodeling work to resolve m:n relationships into n:1 paths, otherwise those measures fall outside generated coverage.

mandates.claim: There are genuinely non-additive measures — ratios and distinct counts across the wrong grain — where you still have to think. 'The USS does not abolish thinking. It removes the busywork so you can spend the thinking where it actually matters.'
mandates.implication: Generation does not cover non-additive measures; they need explicit human handling.

mandates.claim: A hand-built consumption layer scales with the number of questions; a generated one scales with the number of changes to the business model, which is a much slower clock. You model a new entity once, regenerate, and every analysis that can now reach it gets it for free.
mandates.implication: Operating model = model change -> regenerate -> everything downstream updates; consistency becomes a property of the build, not a discipline to enforce.

mandates.claim: 'In practice I generate the USS from a handful of small YAML files, and it takes seconds.'
mandates.implication: Model input is a small set of YAML files; regeneration must be fast enough to be routine (seconds).

mandates.claim: This is the same shift as 'The Rise of the Model-Driven Data Engineer' and 'Contract-Driven Data Transformation': stop writing the artifact, declare the model and generate the artifact.
mandates.implication: Version and review the model declarations, not the generated SQL/tables.

mandates.claim: Query performance was benchmarked, not argued: the same questions were put to a USS and to an equivalent multi-fact star schema on TPC-DS at scale factor 100, and query performance held up — 'There was no meaningful penalty for unifying.'
mandates.implication: Validate USS performance empirically against a multi-fact baseline rather than assuming a penalty; TPC-DS SF100 is the cited reference workload.

mandates.claim: 'It builds fine too: a bridge of roughly a billion rows reloads in about four minutes on an F64, and you can load it incrementally, by key or by updated-at, rather than reloading at all.'
mandates.implication: The bridge build must support incremental loading keyed by business key or by updated-at, with full reload as a fallback rather than the norm.
