quotes: If you run a proper business layer (DAB, in the Daana stack: the layer where you model entities, keys, relationships, and history the way the business actually sees them) then everything a consumption model needs is already declared.
The idea is a single table, the bridge, that connects every entity to every other entity it can legitimately reach.
Instead of one row per entity instance, you make the bridge event-based: one row per measurement event, each carrying its own date.
The rule is short: follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it.
A many-to-many step has no safe direction at all, so the generator skips it and tells you.
Express it as a vendor-neutral semantic contract (e.g. OSI) and any BI tool or AI agent can read it directly.
In practice I generate the USS from a handful of small YAML files, and it takes seconds.
It builds fine too: a bridge of roughly a billion rows reloads in about four minutes on an F64, and you can load it incrementally, by key or by updated-at, rather than reloading at all.
openQuestions: OBT generation source is explicitly left open: 'You can generate it flat, from the model or from the USS.' The builder must pick one.
BI integration is explicitly two-branched: 'You point Power BI, Tableau, or Qlik at the bridge, or build your semantic model on top of it' — the post does not say which to prefer.

The YAML model format is named ('a handful of small YAML files') but no keys, file names, directory layout, or schema are shown anywhere in the post. The DAB YAML contract has to be designed from elsewhere.

'peripherals' is a named component of the USS (`USS` = bridge + peripherals; `data mart` = filter + peripherals) but is never defined — what tables/columns they are, and how they are named, is unspecified.
The semantic-contract format is only exemplified, not fixed: 'a vendor-neutral semantic contract (e.g. OSI)'. Which standard to emit is a decision left to the builder.
How to 'model around' many-to-many relationships in DAB is called out as 'real work' but no technique is given.

How measurement events are declared per entity (which date column maps to order placed / shipped / due, and whether the bridge carries an event-type or stage column) is implied by the event-based grain but never specified.

The relationship between the per-entity build target `order_line.bridge` and the single physical `_bridge` table queried in the SQL is not explained — whether the generator emits one bridge per entity, unioned, or one global table.
How non-additive measures (ratios, distinct counts across the wrong grain) are represented in the sliceability contract — flagged as still requiring thought, but not modeled.
The warning mechanism for skipped many-to-many edges ('the generator skips it and tells you') has no specified output format beyond the `fan-out` field showing `order -> promotion`.

The post says nothing about DAS (Data According to System) or ingestion (no mention of dlt), and names no CLI at all (no daana-cli commands or flags appear). Those parts of the build must be sourced from other posts.
Incremental loading is offered as 'by key or by updated-at' — which strategy applies to which entity/event is left to the implementer.

result.title: The Architectural Blueprint
result.thesis: An architectural blueprint is the overarching, technology-free vision document for a Data Warehouse: it states what the system must achieve (maintainable, scalable, adaptable, good time to market, over a 15-25 year life cycle) and the absolute logical principles that support that vision, with no mention of technology, tooling, process, or modeling method. Its concrete content here is a three-layer logical architecture — DAS (raw, as delivered by the source system), DAB (source-agnostic business semantics), DAR (per-requirement, per-user-group data products) — plus a strict one-directional flow (source → DAS → DAB → DAR → consumers) and a table of per-layer principles stated as absolutes, each with a documented "Why It Matters". The blueprint deliberately contains no exceptions: its job is to act as a gatekeeper that forces an informed, costed decision every time a requirement wants to break a principle, rather than to pre-authorize deviations. It names no technologies, files, commands, schemas or column conventions — so it constrains what DAS/DAB/DAR may contain and how data may move between them, not how to implement them.

mandates.claim: "Data usage for analytical purposes is only allowed from the DAR layer." Reason given: "All analytical consumption goes through DAR so DAB remains a stable, reusable foundation. If users query DAB directly, their usage patterns create implicit dependencies that make the system harder to change."
mandates.implication: The generated Unified Star Schema in DAR must be the only surface exposed to BI tools, notebooks, ad-hoc SQL and any analytical consumer. No end-user or dashboard may be pointed at DAS or at the DAB focal model, however convenient — access must be arranged so DAB has no analytical consumers creating implicit dependencies.

mandates.claim: "Data in the DAR layer can only come from the DAB layer." Reason given: "Every analytical product must be built on business-integrated, quality-assured data. Bypassing DAB means bypassing the single source of truth, leading to inconsistent numbers and eroded trust."
mandates.implication: Every DAR/USS model must select exclusively from DAB relations. No DAR object may read a DAS table, a source system, or a file drop — not even to 'enrich' or 'fill a gap'. A missing attribute in a DAR product is a reason to add it to DAB, never a reason to reach past DAB.

mandates.claim: "Data in the DAB layer can only come from the DAS layer." Reason given: "Clean separation between raw data capture and business integration. DAS absorbs all source-system volatility, so changes in data delivery never force changes in business logic."
mandates.implication: The DAB focal model built with daana-cli must source only from DAS tables. No source connection, API call or external lookup may be wired directly into DAB; anything DAB needs must first be landed in DAS by the ingestion layer.

mandates.claim: DAS principle 'Persist': "Non-volatile. Not allowed to update or delete data." Why It Matters: "The data has to be auditable and the system must be able to reload downstream layers with all historical data at any time."
mandates.implication: dlt ingestion must be append-only. Write dispositions that overwrite or delete (replace, or a merge that physically updates/removes rows) violate the principle; every load must be retained so DAB and DAR can be rebuilt from full DAS history at any time.

mandates.claim: DAS principle 'Simplicity': "Capture and persist only. Transformation logic resides in the code that loads DAB." Why It Matters: "A simple ingestion layer means new sources can be onboarded with minimal effort."
mandates.implication: No cleaning, renaming, casting, deduplication, filtering, joining or business logic in the dlt pipelines — capture the source's raw format as delivered. All transformation belongs in the DAS→DAB code. Onboarding a new source must stay close to a configuration exercise.

mandates.claim: DAS principle 'Metadata': "Every data point entering DAS has to be recorded for auditability." Why It Matters: "Always have the ability to see from where and when data came into the system."
mandates.implication: Every landed record must carry (or be joinable to) provenance metadata answering from where and when it entered. Load-level audit records alone are insufficient if a single data point cannot be traced back to its origin and arrival time.

mandates.claim: DAB principle 'Persist': "Non-volatile. Not allowed to update or delete data." Why It Matters: "Business-integrated data has to be auditable and traceable over time. Immutability ensures we can reproduce any analytical result and understand how business data evolved."
mandates.implication: The DAB focal model must be historized and append-only — no in-place updates, no overwriting of current state, no hard deletes. Any analytical number ever served must be reproducible from DAB as it stood at that time.

mandates.claim: DAB principle 'Reusability': "Produce clear, well-defined atomic business semantics without focus on analytical use-case." Why It Matters: "Straightforward business definitions keep the layer focused on the ability to support any use case."
mandates.implication: Focal-model entities and their definitions must be justifiable without reference to any report, dashboard or ML model. If a DAB construct only makes sense because of one downstream requirement, it belongs in DAR instead.

mandates.claim: DAB principle 'Atomic': "Always has the atomic data point as the base of its semantic meaning." Why It Matters: "Data has to be reusable, independent of analytical use-case. Aggregations happen when data moves to DAR."
mandates.implication: No aggregation, summarization, bucketing or pre-rollup anywhere in DAB; aggregates are computed only in the DAB→DAR step. The post explicitly names a non-atomic DAB as one of the two root causes of teams demanding raw data instead.

mandates.claim: DAB principle 'Business Oriented': "No semantic or structural representation that is source-system specific or use-case specific. Data has a business representation independent of both." Why It Matters: "The system has to adapt to change from both sourcing and usage perspectives. DAB buffers against changes in either from cascading to other layers."
mandates.implication: Names and structures in the focal model must be business terms, not source table/column names, source-system prefixes, source keys, or report/use-case names. Adding a second source for the same concept must not add a parallel structure; swapping a source system out must not change any DAB structure.

mandates.claim: DAB principle 'Metadata': "Every data point entering DAB has to be recorded for auditability." Why It Matters: "Always have the ability to trace data lineage from source through integration, to understand what business rules were applied and when."
mandates.implication: Lineage must be recorded per data point through the integration step, including which business rules were applied and when — not merely which DAS table it came from. Rule versions and effective times must be recoverable.

mandates.claim: DAR principle 'Persist': "Unlike DAS and DAB, DAR structures may be volatile where the requirement demands it (e.g. full refreshes of aggregated views), but all changes must be traceable." Why It Matters: "Reproducibility is essential. Users and auditors need to understand what data was served, when, and how it was derived from DAB."
mandates.implication: DAR is the only layer permitted to be rebuilt or full-refreshed — a generated USS may be dropped and regenerated. But the platform must still record what was served, when, and how it was derived from DAB, so a past delivery can be explained and (given immutable DAB) reproduced.

mandates.claim: DAR principle 'Specialization': "Data structures and data points are specialized to support the specific requirement(s)." Why It Matters: "Data should be easy to use, shaped exactly to what each user group needs."
mandates.implication: Each generated USS is shaped to one requirement set — containing only the data points that requirement needs, in the shape it needs. A general-purpose 'one big model for everyone' in DAR violates the principle.

mandates.claim: DAR principle 'Requirement Oriented': "Contains the exact semantic and structural representation for specific requirement(s). No "reuse" between different requirements. Different user groups must not share structures even when requirements align. No intra-dependencies between requirements of different user groups." Why It Matters: "Reusability in DAB ensures ease of creating unique analytical structures. DAR therefore focuses on specialization per user group, ensuring no contention between requirements. This supports good time to market throughout the system's life cycle."
mandates.implication: Generate a separate USS per user group / requirement even when two groups would produce identical tables — deliberate duplication is required, not a smell. Do not factor out shared conformed dimensions or shared intermediate models across user groups, and never let one group's DAR object depend on another group's DAR object. Reuse belongs in DAB only.

mandates.claim: DAR principle 'Metadata': "Every data point entering DAR has to be recorded for auditability." Why It Matters: "Always have the ability to see what data was delivered to which user group, when, and how it was derived from the business-integrated layer."
mandates.implication: The USS generator must emit metadata tying each delivered data point to a user group, a time, and its DAB derivation — delivery-side audit, not just build logs.

mandates.claim: "The three layers exist to: Break down complexity in code, so data movement between layers has a specific purpose and does not try to do too many things at once. Limit the effects of changes. Each layer's code will not affect the other layers. Specialize each layer so the system avoids sub-optimization."
mandates.implication: Each inter-layer movement is one job: ingest (source→DAS), integrate (DAS→DAB), specialize (DAB→DAR). Code that ingests-and-integrates, or integrates-and-shapes-for-a-report, collapses layers and is disallowed. Layer code must be separable enough that a change in one layer's code does not force edits in another.

mandates.claim: The layer names are chosen deliberately: "DAS/DAB/DAR map roughly to staging/core/marts in dbt terminology, or bronze/silver/gold in the medallion architecture. The concepts overlap, but the naming here is deliberate -- it emphasizes the purpose of each layer (what the data represents) rather than its position in a sequence or a quality grade. That distinction matters when the names are also your principles."
mandates.implication: Name the schemas/layers DAS, DAB, DAR (what the data represents) rather than bronze/silver/gold or staging/core/marts — the name is meant to carry the principle. Treating them as mere renames of medallion tiers loses the point.

mandates.claim: The blueprint states absolutes with reasons and must not contain exceptions: "But if we do not have an absolute principle that is described -- why we have it, what effect it has -- we have nothing to break." And: "Since each "exception" breaks the fundamental principles, it builds a less good system from a maintainability, scalability, and adaptability point of view. Time to market erodes as more exceptions are deployed, and the system's lifetime gets shorter."
mandates.implication: Write each platform principle as an absolute with an explicit 'Why It Matters', and do not build configurable escape hatches, exception flags or 'bypass DAB' modes into the platform or its documentation. Deviations are handled case-by-case as costed, informed decisions — never pre-authorized in code or docs.

mandates.claim: There is no ML/AI raw-data exception: "Machine Learning and AI thrive on well-defined and integrated data, where quality is high and the ML/AI models get a picture of how the company works, not how one system works." The recommended path is "adding the missing data to DAB and building our solution in DAR", because "the ML team ends up re-creating integration work that DAB already handles, but without the benefit of cross-domain consistency or reuse."
mandates.implication: No feature store or ML pipeline may read DAS. ML/AI consumes DAR like every other requirement; missing inputs are added to DAB first. Do not add an ML carve-out to the architecture document or the platform.

mandates.claim: The blueprint is technology-free and overarching: "It contains nothing about technology, processes, modeling methods, or design patterns." "This is not the only architectural document -- it is the overarching one. From it, other documents spawn covering technology, tooling, processes, modeling techniques, and so on. But they should always support the vision statement."
mandates.implication: Tool choices (dlt, daana-cli, the Unified Star Schema, the warehouse engine) belong in subordinate documents, and each must be justified as supporting the vision statement — none may be written into the blueprint itself, and any of them must be replaceable without invalidating it.

mandates.claim: The vision the architecture must serve: "The Data Warehouse has to be Maintainable, Scalable, Adaptable, Good time to market throughout its whole life cycle", where "Maintainable -- Complexity has to be controlled at all times and grow deliberately, not organically", "Scalable -- The system has to grow in data and data concepts without affecting maintainability", "Adaptable -- The system has to handle change of requirements (internal/external, large/small) without affecting maintainability", "Good time to market -- ... Not the fastest way, but always within acceptable timing", and "Throughout its whole life cycle -- Estimated at 15-25 years."
mandates.implication: Design decisions are judged against a 15-25 year horizon, and speed is explicitly not the top criterion — 'the fastest way' is rejected in favour of acceptable timing that upholds the principles. Growth in data volume AND in number of data concepts must not degrade maintainability, which bounds how much bespoke, hand-written per-source or per-report code the platform may accumulate.

mandates.claim: When a requirement does not fit, the blueprint is used to cost the deviation, not to block it: "we do not argue with the reality, we define the cost that the reality wants to impose on us" and "The gatekeeper does not say "no" -- it says "let's understand what this costs us before we decide."" The listed questions include "What time and cost to define and integrate the data needed into DAB?" and "What future value would integrating the data into DAB first give our company and the system?"
mandates.implication: Set up an explicit deviation path: when a requirement forces a break, record which principle is broken, why, how, the effect on maintainability/scalability/adaptability/time-to-market, the reusability lost by short-circuiting the architecture, and the future life-cycle cost — with the product owner, requirement owner, data warehouse architect and data engineer all party to the decision.

artifacts.name: Data According to System (DAS)
artifacts.detail: "Data According to System (DAS) -- Receives and stores data from source systems in its raw format". Elsewhere: "The DAS layer captures data in its raw format and persists it."

artifacts.name: Data According to Business (DAB)
artifacts.detail: "Data According to Business (DAB) -- Data stored semantically and structurally source-system agnostic". Its two stated purposes: "Break dependencies between the sourcing of data and the usage of data." and "Ensure consistency -- the same numbers in all reports when using the same data."

artifacts.name: Data According to Requirement (DAR)
artifacts.detail: "Data According to Requirement (DAR) -- Prepares and structures data for end users based on specific requirements". Elsewhere: "The DAR layer creates and supports data products that user groups want."

artifacts.name: DAS / DAB / DAR ↔ staging / core / marts ↔ bronze / silver / gold
artifacts.detail: "DAS/DAB/DAR map roughly to staging/core/marts in dbt terminology, or bronze/silver/gold in the medallion architecture. The concepts overlap, but the naming here is deliberate -- it emphasizes the purpose of each layer (what the data represents) rather than its position in a sequence or a quality grade. That distinction matters when the names are also your principles."

artifacts.name: Overarching Principles for the Three Layers
artifacts.detail: 1) "Data usage for analytical purposes is only allowed from the DAR layer." 2) "Data in the DAR layer can only come from the DAB layer." 3) "Data in the DAB layer can only come from the DAS layer." Each is stated with an explicit `Reason`. Introduced as: "These are the rules the gatekeeper enforces -- the absolutes we measure every deviation against."

artifacts.name: Principle | Rule | Why It Matters
artifacts.detail: Each layer's principles are documented as a three-column table: the principle's name, the rule stated as an absolute, and why it matters. The 'Why It Matters' column is load-bearing: "if we do not have an absolute principle that is described -- why we have it, what effect it has -- we have nothing to break."

artifacts.name: Persist (DAS principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Non-volatile. Not allowed to update or delete data." Why It Matters: "The data has to be auditable and the system must be able to reload downstream layers with all historical data at any time."

artifacts.name: Simplicity (DAS principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Capture and persist only. Transformation logic resides in the code that loads DAB." Why It Matters: "A simple ingestion layer means new sources can be onboarded with minimal effort."

artifacts.name: Metadata (DAS principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Every data point entering DAS has to be recorded for auditability." Why It Matters: "Always have the ability to see from where and when data came into the system."

artifacts.name: Persist (DAB principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Non-volatile. Not allowed to update or delete data." Why It Matters: "Business-integrated data has to be auditable and traceable over time. Immutability ensures we can reproduce any analytical result and understand how business data evolved."

artifacts.name: Reusability (DAB principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Produce clear, well-defined atomic business semantics without focus on analytical use-case." Why It Matters: "Straightforward business definitions keep the layer focused on the ability to support any use case."

artifacts.name: Atomic (DAB principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Always has the atomic data point as the base of its semantic meaning." Why It Matters: "Data has to be reusable, independent of analytical use-case. Aggregations happen when data moves to DAR."

artifacts.name: Business Oriented (DAB principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "No semantic or structural representation that is source-system specific or use-case specific. Data has a business representation independent of both." Why It Matters: "The system has to adapt to change from both sourcing and usage perspectives. DAB buffers against changes in either from cascading to other layers."

artifacts.name: Metadata (DAB principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Every data point entering DAB has to be recorded for auditability." Why It Matters: "Always have the ability to trace data lineage from source through integration, to understand what business rules were applied and when."

artifacts.name: Persist (DAR principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Unlike DAS and DAB, DAR structures may be volatile where the requirement demands it (e.g. full refreshes of aggregated views), but all changes must be traceable." Why It Matters: "Reproducibility is essential. Users and auditors need to understand what data was served, when, and how it was derived from DAB."

artifacts.name: Specialization (DAR principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Data structures and data points are specialized to support the specific requirement(s)." Why It Matters: "Data should be easy to use, shaped exactly to what each user group needs."

artifacts.name: Requirement Oriented (DAR principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Contains the exact semantic and structural representation for specific requirement(s). No "reuse" between different requirements. Different user groups must not share structures even when requirements align. No intra-dependencies between requirements of different user groups." Why It Matters: "Reusability in DAB ensures ease of creating unique analytical structures. DAR therefore focuses on specialization per user group, ensuring no contention between requirements. This supports good time to market throughout the system's life cycle."

artifacts.name: Metadata (DAR principle)
artifacts.detail: Rule: "Every data point entering DAR has to be recorded for auditability." Why It Matters: "Always have the ability to see what data was delivered to which user group, when, and how it was derived from the business-integrated layer."

artifacts.name: The Vision Statement
artifacts.detail: "The Data Warehouse has to be — Maintainable — Scalable — Adaptable — Good time to market — throughout its whole life cycle." Framed as "the system as an IT artifact -- not detailed business requirements, but what the system itself must achieve". "Each point is then broken down. No technology, no process, no specific use-cases -- just actionable points."

artifacts.name: Maintainable
artifacts.detail: "Complexity has to be controlled at all times and grow deliberately, not organically."

artifacts.name: Scalable
artifacts.detail: "The system has to grow in data and data concepts without affecting maintainability."

artifacts.name: Adaptable
artifacts.detail: "The system has to handle change of requirements (internal/external, large/small) without affecting maintainability."

artifacts.name: Good time to market
artifacts.detail: "The system has to respond to changes and produce value within acceptable time periods, while upholding the fundamental principles. Not the fastest way, but always within acceptable timing."

artifacts.name: Throughout its whole life cycle
artifacts.detail: "Estimated at 15-25 years." Used as the yardstick in the conclusion: "what separates systems that last fifteen years from systems that need replacing in five."

artifacts.name: The three layers exist to:
artifacts.detail: "Break down complexity in code, so data movement between layers has a specific purpose and does not try to do too many things at once." / "Limit the effects of changes. Each layer's code will not affect the other layers." / "Specialize each layer so the system avoids sub-optimization."

artifacts.name: Informed-decision question checklist
artifacts.detail: "What time and cost would it take to build the ML application against raw data?" / "What time and cost to define and integrate the data needed into DAB?" / "What time and cost to build the ML application against DAR?" / "What future value would integrating the data into DAB first give our company and the system?" / "...and many more questions." Weighed alongside: "The cost for the system architecture's life cycle", "The loss of reusability (since we short-circuit the architecture)", "Cost of maintainability, scalability, adaptability, and time to market for the whole system".

artifacts.name: "Machine Learning applications are allowed to use raw data because they will not always work with the data in DAB."
artifacts.kind: anti-pattern (example exception clause NOT to write)
artifacts.detail: Given verbatim as the kind of exception that must never enter the blueprint: "That exception removes the mandate. We have already given the right to bypass the architecture and many fundamental principles."

artifacts.name: Two stated root causes of the 'ML needs raw data' demand
artifacts.detail: "It takes time to define and integrate data into a business representation in DAB." and "The integrated data in DAB is not "atomic" enough, since we have broken the fundamental "Atomic" principle described above."

artifacts.name: Document hierarchy
artifacts.detail: "This is not the only architectural document -- it is the overarching one. From it, other documents spawn covering technology, tooling, processes, modeling techniques, and so on. But they should always support the vision statement." The blueprint itself "contains nothing about technology, processes, modeling methods, or design patterns."

artifacts.name: Deviation stakeholders
artifacts.detail: "the product owner, the requirement owner, the data warehouse architect, and the data engineer" — all named as needing to understand why a principle is broken and what cost it will incur on the system's life cycle.

artifacts.name: (Absent by design)
artifacts.detail: The post names NO file formats, YAML keys, CLI commands or flags, schema/table names, column names, type mappings, SQL constructs or directory layouts. "No mention of technology, modeling methods, or deployment processes -- only the logical approach and the principles that ensure the vision will work."

quotes: Data usage for analytical purposes is only allowed from the DAR layer.
Data in the DAR layer can only come from the DAB layer.
Data in the DAB layer can only come from the DAS layer.
Non-volatile. Not allowed to update or delete data.
Capture and persist only. Transformation logic resides in the code that loads DAB.
Always has the atomic data point as the base of its semantic meaning.
No semantic or structural representation that is source-system specific or use-case specific.
Different user groups must not share structures even when requirements align.
openQuestions: The post names no technology, tooling, modeling method, file format, YAML key, CLI command, schema/table naming convention, column convention, SQL construct or directory layout — by design ("It contains nothing about technology, processes, modeling methods, or design patterns"). Every implementation detail of dlt, daana-cli, the focal model and the Unified Star Schema is deferred to the "other documents [that] spawn" from the blueprint, which the builder must write and justify against the vision statement.

How metadata is physically recorded is unspecified: the rule is only that "Every data point entering [DAS/DAB/DAR] has to be recorded for auditability". Whether that is audit columns on each row, side/audit tables, a catalog, or a log store is left to the builder — as is whether the metadata lives inside the layer or outside it.

How DAR traceability is achieved when DAR is allowed to be volatile is left open: "all changes must be traceable" and users "need to understand what data was served, when, and how it was derived from DAB", but the mechanism (snapshots, versioned outputs, run manifests, rebuild-from-immutable-DAB) is not specified.

The granularity of DAR separation is not settled: the principle speaks both of "specific requirement(s)" and of "user groups" ("Different user groups must not share structures even when requirements align"), so the builder must decide whether a generated USS is scoped per requirement, per user group, or per (user group, requirement) pair — and must define what counts as a 'user group'.

How the 'analytical usage only from DAR' rule is enforced technically (grants/roles, separate databases, tool or network configuration) is not addressed — only that direct DAB querying must not happen because "their usage patterns create implicit dependencies".

What makes DAB "atomic enough" has no stated test, even though a non-atomic DAB is named as a root cause of teams demanding raw data. The builder must define the atomicity criterion for the focal model.
Where "the code that loads DAB" lives and how it is orchestrated is not specified — only that transformation logic must reside there rather than in ingestion.

Whether DAB and DAR are fully rebuilt from DAS history or incrementally maintained is not settled: DAS must let the system "reload downstream layers with all historical data at any time", but the reload/rebuild strategy itself is left to the builder.

Each individual principle break is deliberately left as a per-case open decision: "When a requirement does not fit, we need to take an informed decision" — the blueprint refuses to pre-decide these, and the cost model behind the listed questions ("...and many more questions") is not specified.
The life-cycle horizon is given as an estimate ("Estimated at 15-25 years"), so the exact horizon a given platform designs against is left to the team adopting the blueprint.

result.title: Integration by Design: Analytical Identifiers
result.thesis: Operational systems each own their own identifiers and never have to agree; the moment data is brought together for analytics, that multiplicity becomes the problem of representing one real instance as one instance. The post's answer is the IDFR pattern from the Focal Framework: turn each business identifier into a globally unique, cradle-to-grave "analytical identifier" by prefixing its raw value with a fixed-width Owner+Type code ({Owner}{Type}{Value}, e.g. 4+4 chars, concatenated without a separator), then load every such identifier into a generic per-entity `{ENTITY}_idfr` table that maps many identifiers to one surrogate key. A four-stage pipeline (READER → INTEGRATION → TRUEDELTA → INSERT) LEFT JOINs each of up to five incoming identifier slots against the entire `_idfr` table by value (not by slot position), reuses the matched surrogate key when any slot matches, and mints a fresh UUID when none does. Integration therefore happens at design time in the DAB layer as a property of the identifier itself — not as a downstream reconciliation step, and unlike Data Vault's same-as-link, which defers the reconciliation rather than removing it.

mandates.claim: "This maps to the absolute principles from the architectural blueprint: integration is not a transformation applied after loading - it is a property of the analytical identifier itself, decided at design time, in the DAB layer."
mandates.implication: Identity resolution must be modelled and enforced in the DAB focal model (daana-cli), not implemented as a downstream matching/dedup step in DAR or as post-load SQL. The DAR Unified Star Schema consumes already-resolved surrogate keys; it must never contain resolution logic.

mandates.claim: The analytical system's job is to resolve business identifiers from many sources into analytical identifiers that guarantee one instance. Analytical identifiers must be globally unique (no two instances share one) and must represent the instance from creation to deletion — cradle to grave. Business identifiers need not be globally unique and identify an instance only at a point in time.
mandates.implication: Raw source keys (dlt-landed `account_id`, email, phone) may never be used directly as DAB instance keys. Every source business key must pass through a definition that makes it globally unique and lifecycle-stable before it reaches the identifier table.

mandates.claim: An analytical identifier has three parts — Owner/Issuer, Type, Value — combined into a token `{Owner+Type code}{Value}`, e.g. `G0010001US02079K1079`. "The Owner+Type prefix is fixed-width by design: 4 characters for the Owner, 4 characters for the Type. The exact widths are not the point - what matters is that every Owner and every Type is a unique string of the same length across the system. Concatenation without a separator is then collision-safe by construction."
mandates.implication: The model needs a registry of Owner codes and Type codes, all of identical width per category, enforced at design time. Because widths are fixed and equal, the tool can concatenate prefix+value with no delimiter and no escaping. Variable-width codes would break collision safety, so width uniformity is a validation rule daana-cli should enforce.

mandates.claim: "Once the identifier class (ISIN + STOCK) is mapped to its Owner+Type code, that definition applies everywhere - three systems all sending stock data with ISIN codes produce the same analytical identifier and resolve to the same instance. No per-source matching rules, no manual mapping, no reconciliation at load time."
mandates.implication: Owner+Type codes are declared once per identifier class and reused across every source. Do not build per-source matching rules, a rules table, or a matching engine — the definition is the integration mechanism.

mandates.claim: Key collision is prevented as a side effect, not a separate mechanism: two systems using the raw value "100" for different customers produce `A0010002100` and `A0020002100` — different analytical identifiers, different instances.
mandates.implication: No separate collision-detection or source-qualification step is needed. Distinct source systems must be assigned distinct Owner codes so their identifier spaces stay disjoint by construction.

mandates.claim: "The Owner+Type prefix discipline established earlier is a separate concern: a quality and consistency commitment, recommended as best practice, but not required by the code itself. The pipeline below matches identifier strings byte-for-byte; what those strings encode is the modeller's choice."
mandates.implication: The generated pipeline code contains no knowledge of Owner/Type semantics — it is a plain string equality match. Prefix correctness must therefore be enforced by the modelling layer / review process (daana-cli validation, governance), because the runtime will never catch a bad prefix.

mandates.claim: "Every entity gets an `{ENTITY}_idfr` table - the identifier-to-instance mapping." "The design below is a generic representation; depending on your platform you can add or remove columns or define them differently. Only the IDFR and KEY columns are essential."
mandates.implication: Generate one `{ENTITY}_idfr` table per multi-identifier entity, named from the business entity (INSTRUMENT_idfr, CUSTOMER_idfr). The minimum viable schema is two columns — identifier value and surrogate key; the bookkeeping columns are configurable, so make them template-driven rather than hard-coded.

mandates.claim: "Multiple rows share the same `{ENTITY}_key` - the many-to-one relationship. Three identifiers with the same key = one instance known by three names. The structure is deliberately generic: one column for the value, one for the instance key."
mandates.implication: The `_idfr` table must not be unique on the surrogate key, and must not carry per-source or per-slot columns. One row per (identifier, key) pair. Uniqueness belongs on the identifier value, not on the key.

mandates.claim: "The pattern supports up to 5 identifier slots per entity (`IDFR_01` through `IDFR_05`); unused slots stay NULL." "When an entity legitimately needs a sixth slot beyond the default five, you extend the code by one more slot at every stage of the pipeline. The logic is exactly the same, only the slot count changes. The `_idfr` table itself is untouched and just receives more rows. The cost is a code change, not a schema change"
mandates.implication: Default the generator to 5 slots but parameterise slot count, since every stage's SQL expands symmetrically per slot. Extending slots is a code release, not a migration — the `_idfr` table structure and data stay stable.

mandates.claim: "The pipeline matches identifier values, not slot positions. It searches for matching identifier strings across all slots in the `_idfr` table, regardless of where each one lands in the incoming row. Source column names are irrelevant... The shared ISIN matches because the integration LEFT JOINs each incoming slot against the entire `_idfr` table - not slot-to-slot."
mandates.implication: Generate five independent LEFT OUTER JOINs of the staged row against the whole `_idfr` table (aliases KDW01..KDW05), each on `STG.IDFR_nn = KDW_nn."p_FOCAL01_IDFR"`. Never join IDFR_01 only to slot-1 rows. Slot assignment order may differ per source (Bloomberg puts its ID in IDFR_01, Reuters puts RIC in IDFR_01) and must still resolve.

mandates.claim: "Adding a new way to identify something - a new identifier from a new source, a new identifier type not previously anticipated - only creates new rows. There is no DDL change, no `ALTER TABLE`, no code change to the table itself. You add the new identifier to the transformation logic, redeploy, and the next execution inserts new identifier rows that link to existing instances through shared values."
mandates.implication: Onboarding a new dlt source must never require a DDL migration of `_idfr`. The only change is the identifier transformation expression (the CAST/CONCAT in the READER) plus a redeploy.

mandates.claim: "There is no magic - only relation. A new identifier connects to an existing instance only if the incoming data carries at least one identifier already linked to that instance." "The mechanism is co-occurrence in source data; new identifiers attach to existing instances through the identifiers they share, without any need to know the full set upfront."
mandates.implication: Source extraction must preserve identifier co-occurrence within a single row. A dlt pipeline that splits identifiers across rows/tables, or drops a 'redundant' identifier column, destroys the resolution mechanism. Onboarding a source with no shared identifier will create duplicates by design.

mandates.claim: "The pipeline follows the standard Focal pattern: READER → INTEGRATION → TRUEDELTA → INSERT. Stages are separate for the same reason DAS, DAB, and DAR are separate layers in the architectural blueprint - separation of concerns and testability in isolation."
mandates.implication: Emit four distinguishable stages (as chained CTEs or separate steps), each independently testable. Do not collapse them into one monolithic statement even though they compile into one SQL script.

mandates.claim: Stage roles are fixed: READER extracts up to 5 identifier values into normalised slots; INTEGRATION is "The only stage that reads existing state"; TRUEDELTA splits rows by match outcome (EXISTING_KEY reuses the matched `focal_key` and attaches NEW identifiers in unmatched slots; NEW_KEY gets a fresh `focal_key` (UUID)); INSERT "writes NEW identifiers to `_idfr`. Writes are deferred to the last stage so resolution stays side-effect-free until final."
mandates.implication: No stage before INSERT may write. Resolution must be a pure function of (incoming row, current `_idfr` snapshot), which makes the pipeline re-runnable and testable without side effects.

mandates.claim: "The cost is real. Four stages run before any attribute data is loaded. For an entity with a single, stable primary key, this overhead is unjustified - the pipeline should be skipped entirely. Treat multi-identifier resolution as opt-in: turn it on only for entities that genuinely have multiple, source-spanning identifiers."
mandates.implication: The focal model needs a per-entity flag that turns the IDFR pipeline on. Single-key entities get no `_idfr` table and no four-stage pipeline; defaulting IDFR on for every entity is explicitly wrong.

mandates.claim: "The pipeline is parameter-driven: `'p_*'` strings are substitution placeholders that a templating layer replaces at compile time with actual column or table names, and `{{*}}` are template placeholders for platform-specific syntax (data types, functions like `NOW()` or your key generator)." The post frames this as "The same describe-the-definition-then-generate-the-code shape" also present in the DAS layer.
mandates.implication: daana-cli should compile the IDFR SQL from a declarative model: two placeholder classes — model-level names (`p_*`) resolved from the focal model, and platform-level syntax (`{{STRING}}`, `{{BIGINT}}`, `{{TIMESTAMP}}`, `{{NOW}}`, `{{KEY_GENERATOR}}`) resolved from a target-platform adapter.

mandates.claim: "The symmetric 5-slot expansion and the UNION ALL unpivot below are deliberately platform-neutral - they work on any SQL engine. If your platform offers compact alternatives (`UNPIVOT`, arrays, LATERAL views), feel free to substitute; the logic stays the same." "the pattern is portable: any analytical platform with relational tables and a pipeline orchestrator can carry it, regardless of modelling technique."
mandates.implication: Default code generation to portable UNION ALL unpivoting; platform-specific compaction is an optional adapter optimisation, never a semantic change.

mandates.claim: "The code refers to the surrogate key as `focal_key` throughout - this is the Focal Framework's generic name for the column you saw earlier as `{ENTITY}_key` in the schema and `INSTRUMENT_key` in the walkthrough. The naming is a Focal Framework convention; rename it to whatever fits your code standards."
mandates.implication: The surrogate key column name must be a configurable naming rule in the generator (generic `focal_key` internally vs entity-qualified `{ENTITY}_key` physically), not a hard-coded literal.

mandates.claim: "Downstream tables see the result, not the resolution. A table keyed by `{ENTITY}_key` returns rows from both sources for a single key; the surrogate key is the only thing the rest of the architecture needs to integrate the attribute data." Illustrated by `SELECT * FROM INSTRUMENT_desc WHERE INSTRUMENT_key = 'UUID-ABC';`
mandates.implication: Descriptive/attribute tables and the DAR star schema join only on `{ENTITY}_key`. The `_idfr` table is not part of the query surface for reporting; identifiers are an integration mechanism, not a reporting dimension key.

mandates.claim: "Data Vault uses the same-as-link... But the link does not integrate the instance. You still have two hubs, each with its own surrogate key. The integration is deferred - pushed downstream into queries, satellites, or business-vault logic." "The IDFR pattern resolves identity in one step. Many identifiers map to one instance directly, in a single table, with the Owner+Type prefix doing the integration work at design time. By the time the instance is loaded, it already has one identity. Nothing about it is deferred."
mandates.implication: Do not model identity as hub-per-business-key plus a same-as-link. One table, one surrogate key per instance, resolved before attribute load. Anything that leaves two keys to be reconciled later reintroduces the step this pattern removes.

mandates.claim: Two failure modes are named: "`False unification`: a wrong Owner+Type taxonomy maps two source systems with disjoint identifier spaces to the same prefix, and integration becomes corruption. The prefix is the integration contract - assigning it sloppily is the failure mode." and "`Identifier orphaning`: a new data source arrives with no incoming row that shares an identifier with an existing instance. Resolution creates a duplicate". "These two failure modes are governance concerns at design time."
mandates.implication: Owner+Type assignment needs a governed, reviewed registry — it is a contract, not a naming convenience. Source onboarding needs a design-time check that the new source carries at least one already-known identifier in the same row.

mandates.claim: "At runtime, the `_idfr` table can become corrupt - a false-unification slipped through, source data was wrong, an external writer touched the table, or a new source row brings two previously-independent instances together and reveals they should have been one. The fix is the same in every case: identify the affected rows and repoint the identifiers to their correct keys. Corruption is maintenance, not a flaw in the mechanism."
mandates.implication: Plan an operational repair path that updates `{ENTITY}_key` on affected `_idfr` rows (repointing), and downstream re-keying implied by it. The `row_st` Y/N soft-delete flag and `ver_tmstp` exist to support this kind of maintenance.

mandates.claim: Slot classification is explicit and drives the insert: `exist_new` is 'EXISTING_KEY' when any of the five joined keys is non-null, else 'NEW_KEY'; each `DELTAFILTER_nn` is 'NEW_IDFR' when the slot is non-null but unmatched, 'EXISTING_IDFR' when non-null and matched, NULL otherwise; the final insert filters `WHERE DELTAFILTER = 'NEW_IDFR'`.
mandates.implication: Only previously-unseen identifiers are inserted — the pipeline is idempotent on re-runs of the same source data, and already-known identifiers produce no new rows.

mandates.claim: For EXISTING_KEY rows the matched key is spread across every populated slot: `CASE WHEN IDFR_nn IS NOT NULL THEN COALESCE(focal_key_01, ..., focal_key_05) ELSE NULL END`. Rows with all five slots NULL are excluded (`WHERE COALESCE(IDFR_01, IDFR_02, IDFR_03, IDFR_04, IDFR_05) IS NOT NULL`).
mandates.implication: When several slots match different existing keys, COALESCE silently picks the first non-null — the post does not define a merge for that case, so the generator must at minimum not assume single-match. Rows with no identifiers at all are dropped, never keyed.

mandates.claim: "The Owner+Type prefixes are applied wherever the source values are turned into analytical identifiers, by whatever transformation layer the platform provides." The example applies it inside the READER CAST, e.g. `CONCAT('G0010001', ISIN_code)`.
mandates.implication: Prefixing is a transformation-expression concern that can live at the DAS→DAB boundary (the READER's slot definitions), fed by whatever column names dlt landed — `isin`, `stock_id`, `security_code` are all acceptable inputs because only the produced value matters.

mandates.claim: "The IDFR table structure and the code that loads it - both described below - give you a concrete pattern for key integration that any team can adopt on any analytical platform, regardless of modelling technique." The example "carries only the fundamental logic; handling of timestamps, batch IDs, and other bookkeeping is left to your platform's conventions."
mandates.implication: Treat the published SQL as the semantic core to be generated, and layer your own audit/batch conventions (inst_key/procinst_key population, load timestamps) around it rather than expecting them from the pattern.

artifacts.name: {ENTITY}_idfr
artifacts.detail: "Every entity gets an `{ENTITY}_idfr` table - the identifier-to-instance mapping. The `{ENTITY}` prefix is a placeholder for the business entity you are modelling: an `INSTRUMENT_idfr` table for instruments, a `CUSTOMER_idfr` table for customers, and so on." Shorthand used throughout: `_idfr`.

artifacts.name: {ENTITY}_idfr (column)
artifacts.detail: VARCHAR(255) — "The identifier value". One of the two essential columns.

artifacts.name: eff_tmstp
artifacts.detail: TIMESTAMP(6) — "When this identifier became active"

artifacts.name: ver_tmstp
artifacts.detail: TIMESTAMP(6) — "Version timestamp (for change tracking)"

artifacts.name: row_st
artifacts.detail: VARCHAR(1) — "Row status: Y=active, N=soft-deleted". Insert code hard-codes `'Y' AS row_st`.

artifacts.name: {ENTITY}_key
artifacts.detail: VARCHAR(256) — "The surrogate key - `the instance`". One of the two essential columns. Example instantiation: `INSTRUMENT_key`.

artifacts.name: inst_key
artifacts.detail: BIGINT — "Pipeline execution instance". Populated from `procinst_key AS inst_key`.

artifacts.name: popln_tmstp
artifacts.detail: TIMESTAMP(6) — "When this row was loaded". Set to `{{NOW}}`.

artifacts.name: Only the IDFR and KEY columns are essential
artifacts.detail: "depending on your platform you can add or remove columns or define them differently. Only the IDFR and KEY columns are essential."

artifacts.name: IDFR_01 through IDFR_05
artifacts.detail: "The pattern supports up to 5 identifier slots per entity (`IDFR_01` through `IDFR_05`); unused slots stay NULL." Extending to a 6th slot = "you extend the code by one more slot at every stage of the pipeline".

artifacts.name: {Owner+Type code}{Value}
artifacts.detail: Three parts — Owner/Issuer (who issued it), Type (what kind), Value (the identifier itself) — "Combined into a token: `{Owner+Type code}{Value}`". Example: `G0010001US02079K1079` where `G0010001` is an 8-character code for "ISIN Organization + STOCK type" and `US02079K1079` is the ISIN value.

artifacts.name: Fixed-width prefix: 4 chars Owner + 4 chars Type
artifacts.detail: "The Owner+Type prefix is fixed-width by design: 4 characters for the Owner, 4 characters for the Type. The exact widths are not the point - what matters is that every Owner and every Type is a unique string of the same length across the system. Concatenation without a separator is then collision-safe by construction."

artifacts.name: Owner code series G / A / B / L
artifacts.detail: "the `G` series identifies global registries (ISIN Organization, CUSIP / American Bankers Association, Bloomberg, Reuters); local systems use `A001` through `A999`, rolling into `B` past 999; country-specific issuers use `L` - a Swedish personal number, for example. The convention is a design choice, not a property of the system; what matters is that every Owner is a unique 4-character string."

artifacts.name: Owner codes used in the post
artifacts.detail: `G001` = ISIN Organization; `G002` = CUSIP / American Bankers Association; `G003` = Bloomberg (FIGI); `G004` = Reuters (RIC); `A001` and `A002` = two local/internal systems.

artifacts.name: Type codes used in the post
artifacts.detail: `0001` = STOCK; `0002` = CUSTOMER. Type examples listed in the parts table: STOCK, CUSTOMER, ACCOUNT.

artifacts.name: Worked identifier tokens
artifacts.detail: `G0010001US02079K1079` (ISIN US02079K1079); `G002000102079K107` (CUSIP 02079K107); `G0030001BBG009S3NB30` (FIGI BBG009S3NB30); `G0040001GOOG.OQ` (Reuters RIC GOOG.OQ); `A0010002100` and `A0020002100` (customer "100" in system A vs system B).

artifacts.name: READER → INTEGRATION → TRUEDELTA → INSERT
artifacts.detail: "The pipeline follows the standard Focal pattern: READER → INTEGRATION → TRUEDELTA → INSERT." Stage 1 READER extracts up to 5 identifier values, normalised regardless of source layout. Stage 2 INTEGRATION LEFT JOINs each slot against `_idfr`, marks NEW or EXISTING, retrieves the `focal_key`; "The only stage that reads existing state." Stage 3 TRUEDELTA splits by match outcome. Stage 4 INSERT writes NEW identifiers to `_idfr`.

artifacts.name: idfr_reader
artifacts.detail: Stage 1 CTE. `WITH idfr_reader AS ( SELECT DISTINCT ... FROM "p_SOURCE_PHYSICAL_SCHEMA"."p_SOURCE_TABLE" )` — note the `SELECT DISTINCT`.

artifacts.name: idfr_integration
artifacts.detail: Stage 2 CTE, aliased `STG` for the reader output and `KDW01`..`KDW05` for the five joins to `_idfr`.

artifacts.name: idfr_existing / idfr_new / idfr_delta / idfr_load
artifacts.detail: Stages 3a, 3b, 3c and 4. "The true delta and insert stages unfold across four chained CTEs." Inner unpivot subquery is aliased `UNPIVOTED`.

artifacts.name: exist_new
artifacts.detail: Values `'EXISTING_KEY'` / `'NEW_KEY'`. Computed as: `CASE WHEN (KDW01."p_FOCAL01_KEY" IS NOT NULL OR KDW02... OR KDW05."p_FOCAL01_KEY" IS NOT NULL) THEN 'EXISTING_KEY' ELSE 'NEW_KEY' END AS exist_new`.

artifacts.name: DELTAFILTER_01..05
artifacts.detail: Values `'NEW_IDFR'` / `'EXISTING_IDFR'` / NULL. `CASE WHEN STG.IDFR_nn IS NOT NULL AND KDWnn."p_FOCAL01_KEY" IS NULL THEN 'NEW_IDFR' WHEN STG.IDFR_nn IS NOT NULL AND KDWnn."p_FOCAL01_KEY" IS NOT NULL THEN 'EXISTING_IDFR' ELSE NULL END AS DELTAFILTER_nn`. "The slot-by-slot classification (NEW_IDFR vs EXISTING_IDFR) is stored in `DELTAFILTER_01..05` and used downstream to decide what to insert."

artifacts.name: focal_key
artifacts.detail: "The code refers to the surrogate key as `focal_key` throughout - this is the Focal Framework's generic name for the column you saw earlier as `{ENTITY}_key` in the schema and `INSTRUMENT_key` in the walkthrough. The naming is a Focal Framework convention; rename it to whatever fits your code standards." Per-slot variants: `focal_key_01`..`focal_key_05`; new-key variant: `focal_key_NEW`.

artifacts.name: procinst_key
artifacts.detail: Carried through every stage from the reader (`CAST('p_PROCINST_KEY' AS {{BIGINT}}) AS procinst_key`) and written out as `procinst_key AS inst_key`.

artifacts.name: p_* substitution placeholders
artifacts.detail: "`'p_*'` strings are substitution placeholders that a templating layer replaces at compile time with actual column or table names". Full set in the code: `p_FOCAL01_IDFR01`, `p_FOCAL01_IDFR02`, `p_FOCAL01_IDFR03`, `p_FOCAL01_IDFR04`, `p_FOCAL01_IDFR05`, `p_PROCINST_KEY`, `p_SOURCE_PHYSICAL_SCHEMA`, `p_SOURCE_TABLE`, `p_TARGET_PHYSICAL_SCHEMA`, `p_FOCAL01_IDFRTABLE`, `p_FOCAL01_KEY`, `p_FOCAL01_IDFR`, `p_EFF_TMSTP_DATA`.

artifacts.name: {{*}} platform placeholders
artifacts.detail: "`{{*}}` are template placeholders for platform-specific syntax (data types, functions like `NOW()` or your key generator)". Full set in the code: `{{STRING}}`, `{{BIGINT}}`, `{{TIMESTAMP}}`, `{{NOW}}`, `{{KEY_GENERATOR}}`.

artifacts.name: Reader slot expression
artifacts.detail: `CAST('p_FOCAL01_IDFR01' AS {{STRING}}) AS IDFR_01, -- IDFR_01 definition, for example CONCAT('G0010001', ISIN_code)` and `CAST('p_FOCAL01_IDFR02' AS {{STRING}}) AS IDFR_02, -- IDFR_02 definition, for example CONCAT('G0020001', CU_ID)`. The Owner+Type prefix is applied here, in the CAST.

artifacts.name: Integration join
artifacts.detail: Five separate joins, each against the whole table: `LEFT OUTER JOIN "p_TARGET_PHYSICAL_SCHEMA"."p_FOCAL01_IDFRTABLE" KDW01 ON STG.IDFR_01 = KDW01."p_FOCAL01_IDFR"` … repeated for KDW02..KDW05 with IDFR_02..IDFR_05. "not slot-to-slot".

artifacts.name: EXISTING_KEY key spread
artifacts.detail: `CASE WHEN IDFR_nn IS NOT NULL THEN COALESCE(focal_key_01, focal_key_02, focal_key_03, focal_key_04, focal_key_05) ELSE NULL END AS focal_key_nn` for nn = 01..05. "Spread the matched key across all slots so every IDFR in the row carries the same key."

artifacts.name: Row filters in TRUEDELTA
artifacts.detail: `WHERE COALESCE(IDFR_01, IDFR_02, IDFR_03, IDFR_04, IDFR_05) IS NOT NULL AND exist_new = 'EXISTING_KEY'` (idfr_existing) and the same COALESCE guard with `AND exist_new = 'NEW_KEY'` (idfr_new).

artifacts.name: {{KEY_GENERATOR}} AS focal_key_NEW
artifacts.detail: `{{KEY_GENERATOR}} AS focal_key_NEW, -- a fresh surrogate key from your platform's key generator`. TRUEDELTA: "NEW_KEY (no match anywhere) gets a fresh `focal_key` (UUID)." Walkthrough uses the literal `UUID-ABC`.

artifacts.name: NEW_KEY key propagation
artifacts.detail: `CASE WHEN IDFR_nn IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE focal_key_NEW END AS focal_key_nn` for nn = 01..05, inside `idfr_delta`.

artifacts.name: UNION ALL unpivot
artifacts.detail: Five-branch `SELECT exist_new, IDFR_nn AS IDFR, DELTAFILTER_nn AS DELTAFILTER, focal_key_nn AS focal_key, procinst_key FROM idfr_delta WHERE IDFR_nn IS NOT NULL` joined by `UNION ALL`, aliased `UNPIVOTED`. "Unpivot so each (IDFR, key) becomes its own row". Stated alternatives: "`UNPIVOT`, arrays, LATERAL views".

artifacts.name: WHERE DELTAFILTER = 'NEW_IDFR'
artifacts.detail: Final filter in `idfr_load` — "keep only NEW_IDFR rows for insert".

artifacts.name: eff_tmstp expression
artifacts.detail: `COALESCE(CAST('p_EFF_TMSTP_DATA' AS {{TIMESTAMP}}), {{NOW}}) AS eff_tmstp` — source-supplied effective timestamp, falling back to now.

artifacts.name: INSERT statement
artifacts.detail: `INSERT INTO "p_TARGET_PHYSICAL_SCHEMA"."p_FOCAL01_IDFRTABLE" -- INSERT placement depends on platform syntax` then `SELECT IDFR AS "p_FOCAL01_IDFR", eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp, row_st, focal_key AS "p_FOCAL01_KEY", inst_key, popln_tmstp FROM idfr_load;` — column order matches the table design.

artifacts.name: INSTRUMENT_desc
artifacts.detail: `SELECT * FROM INSTRUMENT_desc WHERE INSTRUMENT_key = 'UUID-ABC'; -- Returns data from BOTH Bloomberg and Reuters sources -- Because both resolved to the same instance through the shared ISIN`

artifacts.name: IDFR row example (identifier / timestamp / status / instance)
artifacts.detail: `G0010001US02079K1079 | 2001-01-01 | ACTIVE | 1`; `G002000102079K107 | 2001-01-01 | ACTIVE | 1`; then `G0030001BBG009S3NB30 | 2001-04-01 | ACTIVE | 1` added later because the source row also carried the already-linked ISIN.

artifacts.name: Key integration vs key collision
artifacts.detail: "`Key integration`: same Owner+Type, same value → same instance." "`Key collision`: same raw value, different meaning → different instances."

artifacts.name: Identity vs Identifier
artifacts.detail: "`Identity` is the representation of a thing as a single instance - not a property of the thing itself." "`Identifier` is a concrete, observable value used to refer to a thing - unique within its data space, but not necessarily covering the thing's full lifecycle." "The relationship is many-to-one: multiple identifiers converge to a single instance." The surrogate key is "the system-generated value that says 'these identifiers all refer to the same instance.'"

artifacts.name: Business identifiers vs Analytical identifiers
artifacts.detail: Business: "Do not need to be globally unique"; "Identify an instance at a specific point in time, not necessarily across its full lifecycle"; "Are what arrives in the source data". Analytical: "Must be globally unique - no two instances can share the same identifier"; "Must represent the instance from creation to deletion - cradle to grave"; "Bridge the messy reality of business identifiers and the clean requirement of unified instances".

artifacts.name: Failure modes: False unification / Identifier orphaning
artifacts.detail: "`False unification`: a wrong Owner+Type taxonomy maps two source systems with disjoint identifier spaces to the same prefix, and integration becomes corruption. The prefix is the integration contract - assigning it sloppily is the failure mode." "`Identifier orphaning`: a new data source arrives with no incoming row that shares an identifier with an existing instance. Resolution creates a duplicate, not because the design failed but because the precondition - co-occurrence in source data - was not met."

artifacts.name: Focal Framework / Focal point / IDFR pattern
artifacts.detail: "the Focal Framework, an analytical modelling approach established in the late 1990s with its own modelling technique called Focal point". The pattern is referred to as "the IDFR pattern" throughout, contrasted with Data Vault's "same-as-link".

artifacts.name: Cross-references
artifacts.detail: "Contract-Driven Data Transformation for the DAS-layer instance" (the same describe-the-definition-then-generate-the-code shape one layer down); "The Rise of the Model-Driven Data Engineer"; "the architectural blueprint" (source of the DAS/DAB/DAR layering and the "absolute principles"); "Focal Framework documentation"; "the AgileData Podcast episode with Shane Gibson".

artifacts.name: Typical 5-identifier sets
artifacts.detail: "a customer might have an internal ID, email, phone, national ID, and a loyalty program number; a financial instrument might have ISIN, FIGI, CUSIP, SEDOL, and a source system ID."

quotes: This maps to the absolute principles from the architectural blueprint: integration is not a transformation applied after loading - it is a property of the analytical identifier itself, decided at design time, in the DAB layer.

The Owner+Type prefix is fixed-width by design: 4 characters for the Owner, 4 characters for the Type. The exact widths are not the point - what matters is that every Owner and every Type is a unique string of the same length across the system. Concatenation without a separator is then collision-safe by construction.
The design below is a generic representation; depending on your platform you can add or remove columns or define them differently. Only the IDFR and KEY columns are essential.
The shared ISIN matches because the integration LEFT JOINs each incoming slot against the entire `_idfr` table - not slot-to-slot. The value creates the connection; the position is incidental.
A new identifier connects to an existing instance only if the incoming data carries at least one identifier already linked to that instance.

For an entity with a single, stable primary key, this overhead is unjustified - the pipeline should be skipped entirely. Treat multi-identifier resolution as opt-in: turn it on only for entities that genuinely have multiple, source-spanning identifiers.

The Owner+Type prefix discipline established earlier is a separate concern: a quality and consistency commitment, recommended as best practice, but not required by the code itself. The pipeline below matches identifier strings byte-for-byte; what those strings encode is the modeller's choice.

When an entity legitimately needs a sixth slot beyond the default five, you extend the code by one more slot at every stage of the pipeline. The logic is exactly the same, only the slot count changes. The `_idfr` table itself is untouched and just receives more rows. The cost is a code change, not a schema change - destructive only in the deployment sense, since a code release is required, but the data and table structure stay stable.
openQuestions: Owner and Type code widths: "The exact widths are not the point" — 4+4 is the example, but the builder must pick widths and then enforce that every code is that exact length.

The Owner code allocation scheme (G for global registries, A001–A999 then B for local systems, L for country-specific issuers) is explicitly "a design choice, not a property of the system" — the builder must define and govern their own registry.

Which columns beyond the identifier value and the surrogate key belong in `{ENTITY}_idfr` — the post says add, remove, or define them differently per platform, so eff_tmstp / ver_tmstp / row_st / inst_key / popln_tmstp are all negotiable.
What to name the surrogate key column: the code uses `focal_key`, the schema uses `{ENTITY}_key` — "rename it to whatever fits your code standards."
Which transformation layer applies the Owner+Type prefix: "by whatever transformation layer the platform provides" (the example puts it in the READER CAST via CONCAT, but that is not mandated).
Which entities get the IDFR pipeline at all — multi-identifier resolution is "opt-in", so the builder must decide per entity where the four-stage cost is justified.

The key generator / surrogate key type: `{{KEY_GENERATOR}}` is "a fresh surrogate key from your platform's key generator"; the walkthrough says UUID and the column is VARCHAR(256), but the choice is left open.

Whether to keep the portable UNION ALL unpivot or substitute a platform-compact form: "If your platform offers compact alternatives (`UNPIVOT`, arrays, LATERAL views), feel free to substitute; the logic stays the same."
Timestamps, batch IDs and other bookkeeping: "handling of timestamps, batch IDs, and other bookkeeping is left to your platform's conventions."
INSERT placement in the statement is flagged as platform-dependent (`-- INSERT placement depends on platform syntax`).

What happens when different slots in one incoming row match different existing instances: the code COALESCEs the first non-null key across slots, and the post only mentions this case obliquely ("a new source row brings two previously-independent instances together and reveals they should have been one") without defining a merge procedure.

How runtime corruption is detected and repaired operationally: the fix is stated as "identify the affected rows and repoint the identifiers to their correct keys", but no detection mechanism, tooling, or downstream re-keying procedure is specified.

How the slot count and per-slot identifier definitions are declared in the model in the first place — the post gives the compiled SQL shape and the `p_FOCAL01_IDFR01..05` placeholders, but not the declarative input format that feeds the templating layer.

result.title: Why Definitions Are the Foundation of Every Data Warehouse
result.thesis: A Data Warehouse's primary job is Information Integration, not storage, performance, or dashboards — and integration has two sides, model integration and semantic integration, of which semantic integration is the hard one. Semantic integration rests entirely on Definitions, organized as a recursive hierarchy: Concept, Characteristic, Domain, Value (plus Terms as labels and Instances as the things that fulfill a Concept's Definition), where every level is itself a Concept needing its own Definition. Without Definitions you cannot determine whether records from two systems describe the same kind of thing, so what you have is "just an expensive copy of source systems." A fourth, organizational constraint is Acceptance: a Definition delivers only the scope it was actually agreed at, so a divisional Definition cannot back an "Enterprise Data Warehouse" claim.

mandates.claim: "the Data Warehouse's primary job is not storage or performance or dashboards. It is Information Integration - creating a shared view of information that works regardless of where the data originated."
mandates.implication: The platform's success criterion is a shared, source-independent view of information — not pipeline throughput, model count, or dashboard delivery. Ingestion (dlt/DAS) and star-schema generation (DAR) are means; the integrated common view is the deliverable.

mandates.claim: "Without clear Definitions, we cannot determine whether data from different systems refers to the same thing. Without that determination, there is no integration - just an expensive copy of source systems."
mandates.implication: A source-shaped landing layer is explicitly NOT integration. Building DAS alone (dlt loading each system's structure) produces the 'expensive copy' the post warns about; the integration verdict is made in the business layer against Definitions.

mandates.claim: Integration has two sides: model integration (how we structure the common view) and semantic integration (what the information actually means); these are tightly intertwined, but semantic integration is where most teams struggle.
mandates.implication: Generating a Unified Star Schema is model integration only. It does not by itself produce integration — the semantic side must be carried explicitly alongside the structure, or the generated model is structurally clean and semantically hollow.

mandates.claim: "A Concept's Definition should answer one question: What is that?" and "A poorly crafted Definition leads to incorrect groupings - records that look similar get integrated despite representing fundamentally different things."
mandates.implication: Every entity in the focal model needs a stored Definition that answers 'What is that?', and that Definition — not structural resemblance between source tables — is what authorizes merging two sources into one entity.

mandates.claim: Semantic Clarity is defined as "the principle that every entity, attribute, relationship, and metric must have clear, business-oriented Definitions accessible to both humans and AI systems across the organization."
mandates.implication: Definitions are required on four object kinds — entity, attribute, relationship, AND metric — not just entities; they must be business-oriented (not technical restatements of column names) and machine-accessible, i.e. stored inside the model artifacts rather than in an external wiki. Note the hierarchy in the article covers Concept/Characteristic/Domain/Value but never names a metric level.

mandates.claim: "The key insight: each Characteristic is its own Concept. We need to define it independently because we need to know what data can legitimately populate it. This recursive principle - that each level in the hierarchy is itself a Concept requiring its own Definition - applies at every level from here on."
mandates.implication: Attributes are first-class definable objects, not annotations on a parent entity. The focal model must support a Definition per attribute, per domain, and per value — the same definition machinery applied recursively at each level.

mandates.claim: A Characteristic holds information that describes an instance of a Concept, but "it is not part of the Definition of 'Customer' itself" (e.g. Concept 'Customer', Characteristic 'Date of Birth').
mandates.implication: Keep the entity's Definition separate from its attribute list; the Definition must not be written as an enumeration of its columns.

mandates.claim: The worked example: Concept "Bank Account", Characteristic "Account Balance", defined as "the balance at a specific point in time, representing the monetary value of settled transactions, not including accrued interest." Without that Definition "we might load values that include unsettled transactions or accrued interest - mixing data with different meanings into the same field."
mandates.implication: The attribute Definition is the acceptance test for which source field may populate it. Source-to-target mapping decisions must be justified against the attribute's Definition, and a source field whose meaning differs (settled vs unsettled, with vs without accrued interest) must not land in that attribute even if names match.

mandates.claim: "Each Characteristic draws its values from a Domain," and a Domain "like every other level, is also a Concept and needs its own Definition." Two main types: Open Domains "require little integration effort"; Closed Domains "often require significant integration work."
mandates.implication: Domain is a modelled object attached to each characteristic, carrying its own Definition, and classified as open or closed — the classification predicts where integration effort lands. Closed-domain characteristics (code lists) need value-level integration work planned; open-domain ones (Date) need only format work.

mandates.claim: "Values within a Domain also need a defined format. A date must follow its specified format regardless of how the source system stored it. Format integration is mechanical, but skipping it breaks downstream consistency."
mandates.implication: Format normalization on the way from source structure to the business model is mandatory, not optional, and the target format is a property of the Domain — the source system's storage format never wins.

mandates.claim: Individual Values can be their own Concepts with their own Definitions (GICS code "10" = Term "Energy Sector" with a full prose definition; "The same applies to ISO 4217 Currency Codes, where each code carries a Definition"), and "The ability to integrate Values - not just Concepts, Characteristics, and Domains - is what completes the common information view in the Data Warehouse."
mandates.implication: Reference/code tables must carry a per-value Definition, and cross-system code values must be integrated to a common set. Stopping integration at the entity/attribute level leaves the common view incomplete.

mandates.claim: "A Term is simply a name... Terms are how we communicate, but they are not how we understand." "Two systems might use different Terms for the same Concept, or - more dangerously - the same Term for different Concepts. Without explicit Definitions, we cannot tell which case we are looking at."
mandates.implication: Never integrate on name match. Automated or AI-assisted mapping that aligns source columns by label is exactly the failure mode described; the model must keep Term (label) and Definition (meaning) as separate fields so a Term collision can be detected.

mandates.claim: "An Instance is an individual thing that fulfills the Definition of a Concept... The only way to determine whether something qualifies is to check it against the Concept's Definition."
mandates.implication: The predicate deciding which source rows become instances of a business entity (filters, row-level selection criteria) must be derivable from and traceable to that entity's Definition.

mandates.claim: "A Definition's usability depends on how widely it is accepted. A Definition created for a single division cannot serve as an Enterprise Definition." "If someone claims an 'Enterprise Data Warehouse,' the Definitions must be accepted throughout the enterprise. They seldom are."
mandates.implication: Acceptance scope is metadata that belongs with each Definition, and the scope a deliverable is advertised at must not exceed the scope of the Definitions behind it. Being "explicit about acceptance scope - and honest about its limitations - is essential for realistic expectations."

mandates.claim: "Where to start? Before integrating data from two systems, write down the Definition of each shared Concept and verify that both teams agree on it. If they do not, you have found the exact place where integration will break."
mandates.implication: Definition-writing and cross-team agreement precede the integration build for each shared Concept; disagreement is a discovered risk to surface, not a blocker to route around.

mandates.claim: When Concept, Characteristics, Domains, and Values "are all integrated according to their Definitions, the information becomes usable throughout the organization - regardless of which system or country created it. That is the primary purpose of a Data Warehouse."
mandates.implication: All four levels must be integrated for the result to count — partial integration (entities only, or entities plus attributes) does not reach the stated goal.

artifacts.name: Concept
artifacts.detail: Verbatim from the hierarchy list: "`Concept` - What kind of thing are we describing?" Also: "A Concept represents a 'kind of thing.'... While the Concept itself never exists in the real world, it carries the Definition we rely on to sort and interpret information." In the Conclusion it appears as "`Concept Definition` - what kind of thing is this?"

artifacts.name: Characteristic
artifacts.detail: "`Characteristic` - What properties describe instances of this Concept?" Defined as "information that describes an instance of a Concept." Conclusion form: "`Characteristic Definition` - what describes instances of this Concept?"

artifacts.name: Domain
artifacts.detail: "`Domain` - What values can a Characteristic take?" Conclusion form: "`Domain Definition` - what values are valid, and in what format?"

artifacts.name: Value
artifacts.detail: "`Value` - What does a specific value within a Domain mean?" Conclusion form: "`Value Definition` - what does a specific value mean?"

artifacts.name: Term
artifacts.detail: "the labels we refer to Concepts by"; "A Term is simply a name - a word or group of words that refers to a Concept." Described as a "knowledge bearer" for those who already know the Definition behind it.

artifacts.name: Instance
artifacts.detail: "the individual things that fulfill a Concept's Definition"; "a specific bank account, a particular customer, an individual organization."

artifacts.name: Semantic Clarity
artifacts.detail: "the principle that every entity, attribute, relationship, and metric must have clear, business-oriented Definitions accessible to both humans and AI systems across the organization." Also a tag on the post.

artifacts.name: Information Integration
artifacts.kind: named discipline / stated purpose of the DW
artifacts.detail: "creating a shared view of information that works regardless of where the data originated"; "the discipline of determining which Concept each data record belongs to."

artifacts.name: model integration
artifacts.detail: "how we structure the common view" — the structural side (maps to generating a schema).

artifacts.name: semantic integration
artifacts.detail: "what the information actually means" — "where most teams struggle - and it is the focus of this article."

artifacts.name: Open Domains
artifacts.detail: "`Open Domains` require little integration effort. Date is a good example - 'Date of Birth' takes values from the Date Domain. The values themselves do not need integration; only the format does."

artifacts.name: Closed Domains

artifacts.name: ISO 4217 Currency Code

artifacts.name: Global Industrial Classification System (GICS)

artifacts.name: GICS code "10" — "Energy Sector"
artifacts.detail: "Companies whose businesses are dominated by the construction or provision of oil rigs, drilling equipment, energy-related services, or the exploration, production, marketing, refining, and transportation of oil, gas, coal, and other consumable fuels."

artifacts.name: Concept "Bank Account" / Characteristic "Account Balance"
