artifacts.name: Concept "Customer" / Characteristic "Date of Birth" / Date Domain
artifacts.detail: "If the Concept is 'Customer,' a Characteristic might be 'Date of Birth.' That value describes a specific customer, but it is not part of the Definition of 'Customer' itself." Date of Birth "takes values from the Date Domain."

artifacts.name: "mixing apples with pears"
artifacts.detail: "mixing data with different meanings into the same field. Practitioners call this 'mixing apples with pears,' and it leads to reporting that looks correct but produces wrong conclusions."

artifacts.name: Enterprise Definition / "Enterprise Data Warehouse"
artifacts.detail: "A Definition created for a single division cannot serve as an Enterprise Definition." "If someone claims an 'Enterprise Data Warehouse,' the Definitions must be accepted throughout the enterprise. They seldom are."

artifacts.name: acceptance scope
artifacts.detail: "Being explicit about acceptance scope - and honest about its limitations - is essential for realistic expectations." The post frames scope mismatch as "one of the most common problems in practice - expectations about data usability that exceed the scope of the Definitions behind it."

artifacts.name: "Definitions in Information Management" by Malcolm D. Chisholm, Ph.D.
artifacts.detail: Recommended "For a deeper treatment of Definitions and their management - including formal methods for creating, validating, and governing them across an organization... It remains one of the clearest formal frameworks on this subject."

artifacts.name: Three-part series structure
artifacts.detail: Part 1 (this post): "what Definitions are and why they form the foundation of any Data Warehouse." Part 2: "how Definitions are applied in practice when doing integration work: where they break down, how teams negotiate them, and what happens when they are missing." Part 3: "how this integration discipline translates into declarative architectures and AI-driven platforms." The DAS/DAB/DAR build guidance is deferred to Part 3.

artifacts.detail: data-warehousing, data-modeling, semantic-clarity, integration, methodology

quotes: But the Data Warehouse's primary job is not storage or performance or dashboards. It is Information Integration - creating a shared view of information that works regardless of where the data originated.

Without clear Definitions, we cannot determine whether data from different systems refers to the same thing. Without that determination, there is no integration - just an expensive copy of source systems.

This requirement for clear Definitions is what we call Semantic Clarity - the principle that every entity, attribute, relationship, and metric must have clear, business-oriented Definitions accessible to both humans and AI systems across the organization.

The key insight: each Characteristic is its own Concept. We need to define it independently because we need to know what data can legitimately populate it. This recursive principle - that each level in the hierarchy is itself a Concept requiring its own Definition - applies at every level from here on.

Values within a Domain also need a defined format. A date must follow its specified format regardless of how the source system stored it. Format integration is mechanical, but skipping it breaks downstream consistency.
The ability to integrate Values - not just Concepts, Characteristics, and Domains - is what completes the common information view in the Data Warehouse.
A Definition's usability depends on how widely it is accepted. A Definition created for a single division cannot serve as an Enterprise Definition.

Before integrating data from two systems, write down the Definition of each shared Concept and verify that both teams agree on it. If they do not, you have found the exact place where integration will break.
openQuestions: The post asks its own unanswered question about acceptance: "The hierarchy above assumes Definitions already exist and are agreed upon. But agreed upon by whom, and at what scope?" It insists scope be explicit but never says how to record or govern it — a builder must decide the representation (a scope field per definition? per model? an approver list?).

How Definitions are made "accessible to both humans and AI systems" is asserted as a requirement but never specified — no format, storage location, key name, or serialization is given. The DAB focal model's definition-carrying mechanism is entirely a builder choice.

Semantic Clarity requires definitions on "entity, attribute, relationship, and metric," but the four-level hierarchy (Concept / Characteristic / Domain / Value) contains no relationship or metric level. How relationships and metrics fit the hierarchy — and what their Definitions must answer — is left open.

Domains need "a defined format," but no format-specification syntax, type system, or DAS→DAB type-mapping rule is offered. Where format normalization executes (dlt ingestion vs. the business layer) is unresolved.

Open vs Closed is presented as "two main types" of Domain with hedged language ("require little" / "often require significant"), implying other types exist and that the classification may not be a clean binary flag.

The post says definition disagreement between two teams locates "the exact place where integration will break" but gives no resolution procedure — whether to split into separate Concepts, escalate, or narrow the acceptance scope is undecided.

Whether Value-level integration means mapping every source code to a shared standard (ISO 4217, GICS) or defining a bespoke common Domain per Concept is not settled; only that Values must be integrated.

The post never mentions DAS, DAB, DAR, dlt, daana-cli, or the Unified Star Schema. The mapping from this hierarchy onto a three-layer declarative architecture is explicitly deferred to Part 3 ("how this integration discipline translates into declarative architectures and AI-driven platforms").

result.title: daana-cli 0.7.0: foundation rework, ~2× faster, full-refresh, M:N relationships and more!
result.thesis: A release post for daana-cli 0.7.0, framed as a "foundation rework" of the DAB engine. It removes the local Postgres sidecar so everything runs inside a single Go binary, moves batch lifecycle tracking from local CSV files into a warehouse `batch_history` table, adds `--full-refresh` scoped to workflow/entity/attribute, relaxes YAML naming to any casing while lowercasing all framework-generated columns and table suffixes, and rewrites many-to-many relationship views from pair-oriented to set-oriented. Several of these are breaking changes to the exact contract a DAR layer reads: lowercase framework columns, set-semantics on `view_<source>_has_<target>`, value-run compaction on `view_<entity>_hist`, and BigQuery partitioning/clustering tuned for a `WHERE ver_tmstp > last_run_tmstp` incremental DAR build. The post explicitly endorses the DAS → DAB → DAR three-layer setup as the thing that keeps a DAB rebuild from being visible to BI.

mandates.claim: The post names the recommended architecture as a three-layer setup, DAS → DAB → DAR, and says that under it only the DAB layer rebuilds during the 10-15 minute drop-and-redeploy, with DAR and downstream BI consumers noticing nothing as long as the rebuild completes within their refresh interval; 'If you query DAB directly from BI, plan a window accordingly.'
mandates.implication: DAR must be a materialized layer that survives a DAB drop-and-redeploy, and BI must be pointed at DAR, not at DAB tables/views. Pointing BI at DAB forfeits the no-downtime property and forces a scheduled maintenance window. DAR refresh interval must be longer than ~15 minutes for the rebuild to be invisible.

mandates.claim: All Daana-generated column names (`eff_tmstp`, `ver_tmstp`, `type_key`, `data_key`, `inst_key`, `row_st`, `inst_row_key`, `popln_tmstp`) and table suffixes (`_idfr`, `_desc`, `_x`) now use lowercase. This is called out as a breaking change for downstream consumers.
mandates.implication: Every generated USS/DAR query, view, and column reference must address framework columns and suffixes in lowercase. Any DAR generator template carrying UPPERCASE framework names must be audited and updated before redeploying.

mandates.claim: On BigQuery, `_desc` and `_x` tables are partitioned via `PARTITION BY RANGE_BUCKET(type_key, ...)` and cluster keys are restructured to favor `ver_tmstp` (system load time) over `eff_tmstp` (business time). The post states this 'enables incremental DAR / data-mart builds via the `WHERE ver_tmstp > last_run_tmstp` pattern as a clustered range scan.'
mandates.implication: The DAR incremental build predicate should be `WHERE ver_tmstp > last_run_tmstp`, not a predicate on `eff_tmstp`. Filtering DAR increments on business time defeats the clustering and scans more bytes. The DAR layer must persist a `last_run_tmstp` watermark of its own.

mandates.claim: `view_<source>_has_<target>` now returns the active member set per source entity at the latest effective timestamp. The previous pair-oriented partitioning returned one row per source/target pair; the new partitioning ties all members of the latest set together so the view returns them as one set. Customers running INCREMENTAL pipelines on M:N relationships may see different row counts than before, and the new counts are the correct ones.
mandates.implication: DAR bridge tables built from `view_<source>_has_<target>` get set semantics, not pair semantics. Any DAR row-count reconciliation or test baseline taken from a pre-0.7.0 build is invalid. Do not assume one row per source/target pair.

mandates.claim: Under INCREMENTAL, relationship pipelines no longer write `row_st = 'N'` rows for set transitions; set membership changes are detected by the set-oriented view at query time rather than by row-level closer/opener emission. FULL_LOG continues to soft-delete rows for source-row disappearance.
mandates.implication: DAR logic must not detect relationship membership changes by reading `row_st = 'N'` rows out of `_x` tables under INCREMENTAL — those rows are no longer emitted. Read the set-oriented view instead. The behavior differs between INCREMENTAL and FULL_LOG, so the DAR generator cannot assume one uniform relationship-change mechanism.

mandates.claim: `view_<entity>_hist` returns one row per value-run: entity history views apply gaps-and-islands compaction, consecutive observations of the same attribute tuple collapse into one row anchored at the earliest observed effective timestamp for that value-run. `COUNT(*)`, `AVG`, and `SUM` over the view now treat each value-state as one observation rather than each ingest event. 'Audit consumers that need every observation should query `<entity>_desc` directly.'
mandates.implication: Choose the DAR source per use case: `view_<entity>_hist` for value-state analytics (SCD-style change history), `<entity>_desc` for audit/ingest-event-level grain. Aggregates over `_hist` count value-states, not ingests — a DAR fact built on `_hist` cannot answer 'how many times was this loaded'.

mandates.claim: `--full-refresh` operates at three scopes: full workflow (`daana-cli execute --full-refresh`), a single entity (`--entity X`), or one attribute (`--attribute Y`). '`--entity` requires `--full-refresh`. `--attribute` requires `--entity`. Names are validated via the same SSOT used by the linter.'
mandates.implication: Operational runbooks can rebuild a slice without dropping the DWH. The flag dependency chain is strict — `--entity` alone or `--attribute` alone is invalid. Entity/attribute names passed on the CLI must match the model SSOT the linter uses.

mandates.claim: Entity IDs, workflow IDs, attribute names, and relationship names accept any casing (lowercase, UPPERCASE, Mixed_Case, mixedCase); the checker and compiler previously enforced UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. 'Names must still be valid SQL identifiers: letters, digits, underscores. Hyphens are no longer accepted.' Model YAML names are preserved exactly as written; cross-reference lookups are case-insensitive at compile time; compiled output uses the model's canonical casing.
mandates.implication: Names in DAB YAML may use any house casing convention, but hyphens are forbidden and only letters/digits/underscores are legal. Cross-references between YAML files need not match casing. The DAR generator must read the model's canonical casing (as written in YAML) to predict compiled object names — it cannot assume UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

mandates.claim: The lint warnings `entity-name-casing`, `attribute-type-casing`, and `relationship-name-casing` were removed.
mandates.implication: The linter no longer enforces a naming-casing house style. Any casing convention for the DAB model must be enforced by team convention or external CI checks, not by daana-cli.

mandates.claim: Everything now runs inside the Go binary itself. The local Postgres sidecar is gone — no external database, no Docker port, no second process. `install` no longer has a `local` subcommand (`install remote` is now just `install`), `daana-cli reset` is gone, and the legacy execution-mode flag is gone; the in-process path is the only path.
mandates.implication: Provisioning for the DAB layer is a single executable — no Docker sidecar, no port allocation, no local database service in CI. Any scripts calling `install local`, `install remote`, `daana-cli reset`, or the execution-mode flag must be rewritten.

mandates.claim: Every pipeline execution is tracked in a `batch_history` table in the warehouse with a status lifecycle `Running` → `Complete` / `Failed`. 'Failed pipelines don't advance the watermark.' Stale runs from crashes are auto-recovered via DW reconciliation. The old local CSV batch tracking (`~/.daana/batch/`) is replaced by this, and it works from CI/CD, containers, and across team members.
mandates.implication: Batch state is warehouse-resident, so the same DAB workflow can be executed from a laptop, CI/CD, or a teammate's machine without transferring local state. Do not depend on or migrate `~/.daana/batch/`. Watermark advancement is safe on failure — a failed run does not silently skip data.

mandates.claim: `--force` on execute overrides stale run detection when a previous execution appears stuck from a crash, and `batch_stale_timeout` in workflow advanced settings is a configurable timeout (default 8h) for stale run detection; pipelines running longer than this are auto-recovered on the next execution.
mandates.implication: Long-running DAB workflows need `batch_stale_timeout` tuned above their real runtime or they will be auto-recovered mid-flight. CI orchestration needs a documented `--force` escape hatch for crashed runs.

mandates.claim: Per-table `batch_expression` in mapping YAML overrides the workflow-level batch expression on individual tables when source tables use different timestamp columns or require custom SQL.
mandates.implication: A dlt-landed DAS schema with heterogeneous load/update timestamp columns per table does not need one uniform column — set `batch_expression` per mapping table. But it must be set per table wherever the DAS timestamp column diverges from the workflow default.

mandates.claim: DATE source columns no longer fail batch filtering: the generated filter casts the column to `TIMESTAMP` and wraps batch values in `TIMESTAMP()`. Cross-project `batch_expression` validation now runs correctly when the source project differs from the target project.
mandates.implication: DAS landing tables may expose DATE-typed batch columns without a pre-cast, and on BigQuery the DAS project may differ from the DAB target project.

mandates.claim: Relationship-only mapping tables are now supported — mapping tables can declare relationships without any attributes; previously such tables were rejected with an empty-attributes validation error.
mandates.implication: dlt-generated junction/child tables that carry only foreign keys can be mapped directly as pure relationship sources, with no synthetic attribute needed to satisfy validation.

mandates.claim: A new `TypeTextDDL` atom provides unlimited-length string columns, mapping to `text` (PostgreSQL), `STRING` (BigQuery / Snowflake), `CLOB` (Oracle), `VARCHAR(MAX)` (MSSQL). 'Use for free-text fields where a fixed length is impractical.'
mandates.implication: Free-text DAS columns (JSON blobs, descriptions, notes landed by dlt) map to `TypeTextDDL` rather than an arbitrarily large fixed-length type.

mandates.claim: MSSQL and Oracle dialects fail fast with a clear 'not yet supported' error at config load, factory time, preflight, and every other entry point; previously they fell through silently to the PostgreSQL executor, producing wrong-syntax SQL and unpredictable corruption. They remain in the connection-profile schema under a `PlannedDialects` list so profiles can be authored in advance. Tested environments are latest PostgreSQL and current GCP-default BigQuery.
mandates.implication: Target warehouse for a DAB/DAR build must be PostgreSQL or BigQuery. MSSQL/Oracle connection profiles can be written now but will not run. Snowflake appears in the type mapping and truncate handling but is not listed among tested environments.

mandates.claim: Existing BigQuery customers should drop and redeploy their data warehouse to benefit from the partitioning changes; PostgreSQL is unchanged. The upgrade from any pre-0.7.0 build is a standard drop-and-redeploy: update the binary/image, drop the metadata schema and the data warehouse schema, then `daana-cli install` → `daana-cli deploy` → `daana-cli execute`, taking roughly 10-15 minutes for a full DWH, and 'Runs are idempotent.'
mandates.implication: The DAB bootstrap/redeploy sequence is exactly install → deploy → execute against an empty metadata schema and empty DWH schema. Automation can safely re-run it. BigQuery deployments must be rebuilt to pick up partitioning; PostgreSQL deployments need not be for that reason.

mandates.claim: 'State preservation: drop-and-redeploy doesn't touch your YAML. Models, mappings, workflows, connection profiles - the source of truth lives in your version-controlled YAML, and the new build regenerates everything from it.'
mandates.implication: All DAB definitions — models, mappings, workflows, connection profiles — must live in version-controlled YAML; the warehouse holds no authoritative state that a rebuild would lose. Nothing may be hand-edited in the warehouse.

mandates.claim: The deploy sequence is now 5 phases: Staging DDL → Entity DDL → Populate metadata staging → Execute metadata pipeline → Function DDL. Function DDL runs last so semantic views embed `type_key` values read from the metadata tables rather than sequential counters.
mandates.implication: `type_key` values are derived from metadata tables at deploy time, not from a stable sequential counter. DAR must not hardcode `type_key` literals or assume they are stable across deploys — read them from the metadata tables or the semantic views.

mandates.claim: Entity key columns in metadata tables widened to `VARCHAR(256)` (previously `BIGINT`); `type_key`, `data_key`, `inst_key`, and the batch-lifecycle keys remain `BIGINT`. See ADR-109 for the rationale.
mandates.implication: DAR join/column typing must treat entity key columns as VARCHAR(256) strings and the four listed keys as BIGINT. Any DAR schema that declared entity keys as integers must change.

mandates.claim: Pre-DAANA-97 binaries silently broke INCREMENTAL relationship processing on any model change after deploy; customers who previously ran `deploy` without a clean install may have orphan relationships in their `_x` tables, with the symptom 'data looks fine, but relationships don't update.' `daana-cli execute --full-refresh --entity X` per affected entity is the less invasive recovery path if you want to avoid a full drop-and-redeploy.
mandates.implication: A `deploy` after a model change is not sufficient on pre-0.7.0 builds; on 0.7.0, orphan `_x` rows have a documented per-entity recovery. Relationship staleness is a real failure mode to test for, not a theoretical one.

mandates.claim: The engine validates generated index / table / schema names against PostgreSQL's 63-character limit, with a clear error and suggested fix. The test harness auto-discovers source schemas, so typos in mapping `source_table` references are caught with a validation error showing the closest match.
mandates.implication: Entity/attribute naming must stay short enough that generated index/table/schema names fit in 63 characters on PostgreSQL. `source_table` values are validated against the real DAS schema, so DAS must be reachable/discoverable at validation time.

mandates.claim: Parallel workers default was raised from 4 to 8, the metadata pipeline now runs in parallel across those 8 workers (metadata loading on BigQuery is 3-4× faster), and PROCINST key caching eliminates roughly 10 minutes of redundant pipeline-SQL regeneration per execute on BigQuery.
mandates.implication: Default concurrency against the target warehouse is 8 workers — size warehouse connection limits / BigQuery slot expectations accordingly.

mandates.claim: Late-arrival rows for TYPE_TABLE attributes are now captured at their own effective time; previously late arrivals could be silently dropped because the truedelta compared the earliest source row against the target's chronologically-latest row regardless of timestamp, and rows with matching values were marked NOCHANGE and never inserted. INCREMENTAL truedelta is aligned with FULL_LOG for exact-tuple modeling, and within-batch transitions now emit historical rows correctly.
mandates.implication: A DAS source that can deliver out-of-order/late rows (a common dlt reality) is now handled under INCREMENTAL for TYPE_TABLE attributes. Row counts in history for such sources will legitimately differ from pre-0.7.0 baselines.

mandates.claim: Dialect-aware `TRUNCATE TABLE`: BigQuery and Snowflake get per-table truncate statements; PostgreSQL keeps multi-table truncate.
mandates.implication: No action for model authors, but any custom teardown tooling written alongside DAB must not issue PostgreSQL-style multi-table TRUNCATE against BigQuery/Snowflake.

mandates.claim: Transient BigQuery errors are retried via a new `bqretry` SSOT package; `jobBackendError` and `jobInternalError` are classified as transient and retried with exponential backoff across executors, metadata read, preflight, query, table-exists, and storage-write API paths.
mandates.implication: BigQuery transient-error retry is handled inside daana-cli for those two error classes — do not layer an outer retry loop that would duplicate work; orchestration retries should target hard failures only.

artifacts.name: docs.daana.dev
artifacts.detail: Rebuilt in 0.7.0: local search, redesigned tutorial flow, new pages on advanced mapping patterns, expanded glossary, unified brand presentation; CI validates link integrity on every prebuild.

artifacts.name: drop the metadata schema and the data warehouse schema
artifacts.detail: Migration sequence: update the daana-cli image / binary; drop the metadata schema and the data warehouse schema; `daana-cli install` → `daana-cli deploy` → `daana-cli execute`. "roughly 10-15 minutes for a full DWH. Runs are idempotent."

quotes: With the recommended three-layer setup (DAS → DAB → DAR), only the DAB layer rebuilds during the 10-15 minutes. DAR and downstream BI consumers don't notice anything as long as the rebuild completes within their refresh interval. If you query DAB directly from BI, plan a window accordingly.
This reduces bytes scanned on analytical queries and enables incremental DAR / data-mart builds via the `WHERE ver_tmstp > last_run_tmstp` pattern as a clustered range scan.

All Daana-generated column names (`eff_tmstp`, `ver_tmstp`, `type_key`, `data_key`, `inst_key`, `row_st`, `inst_row_key`, `popln_tmstp`) and table suffixes (`_idfr`, `_desc`, `_x`) now use lowercase, following modern SQL convention.

`view_<source>_has_<target>` now returns the active member set per source entity at the latest effective timestamp. The previous pair-oriented partitioning returned one row per source/target pair; the new partitioning ties all members of the latest set together so the view returns them as one set.

`COUNT(*)`, `AVG`, and `SUM` over the view now treat each value-state as one observation rather than each ingest event. Audit consumers that need every observation should query `<entity>_desc` directly.

Names must still be valid SQL identifiers: letters, digits, underscores. Hyphens are no longer accepted. Model YAML names are preserved exactly as written; cross-reference lookups are case-insensitive at compile time; compiled output uses the model's canonical casing.
`--entity` requires `--full-refresh`. `--attribute` requires `--entity`. Names are validated via the same SSOT used by the linter.
Every pipeline execution is now tracked in a `batch_history` table with a status lifecycle: `Running` → `Complete` / `Failed`. Failed pipelines don't advance the watermark.
openQuestions: The post says the maintenance window "depends on your architecture" — you must decide whether BI reads DAR (invisible rebuild) or queries DAB directly (plan a window). It does not say how DAR should be materialized or refreshed to achieve this.

The linter no longer enforces UPPER_SNAKE_CASE and the three casing lint rules were removed, so a house naming convention for entity IDs, workflow IDs, attribute names and relationship names is now an open team choice (only constraint: letters, digits, underscores; no hyphens).

INCREMENTAL vs FULL_LOG is left as a per-pipeline choice, and the two now have materially different relationship semantics (forward-only emission with query-time set detection vs. soft-delete on source-row disappearance). The post does not say which to pick.
Whether DAR reads `view_<entity>_hist` (one row per value-run, compacted) or `<entity>_desc` (every observation) is an explicit consumer-side choice the post surfaces but does not decide.
Recovery from orphan relationships in `_x` tables is a stated choice between a full drop-and-redeploy and `daana-cli execute --full-refresh --entity X` per affected entity.
`batch_stale_timeout` defaults to 8h and is described as configurable in workflow advanced settings; the correct value for a given workflow's real runtime is left to the operator.

Per-table `batch_expression` overrides are offered for sources with different timestamp columns or custom SQL, but the post gives no rule for when a DAS source warrants an override versus using the workflow-level expression.

Snowflake's support level is unresolved: it appears in the `TypeTextDDL` mapping and in dialect-aware `TRUNCATE TABLE`, but the tested environments listed are only PostgreSQL and BigQuery, and only MSSQL/Oracle are named under `PlannedDialects`.

PostgreSQL's 63-character generated-identifier limit is enforced, but the post does not document how entity/attribute/relationship names compose into generated index/table/schema names, so a safe name-length budget must be determined empirically.

Nothing in the post describes DAR/Unified Star Schema generation itself — it only fixes the DAB read contract (lowercase framework columns, set-oriented relationship views, value-run history views, `ver_tmstp` clustering, VARCHAR(256) entity keys) that a DAR generator must consume.

`type_key` values are read from metadata tables at Function DDL time rather than being sequential counters; the post does not state whether those values are stable across redeploys, which matters if DAR persists them.

result.title: The Rise of the Model-Driven Data Engineer
result.thesis: Data engineering is shifting from hand-writing SQL/Python transformations to declaring semantic intent in YAML and generating the code from it — the same move IaC made for ops and OpenAPI made for APIs. The post's concrete proposal is a three-layer, fully declarative platform: DAS (Data As System sees it — landing + staging, driven by data contracts), DAB (Data As Business sees it — entities and relationships declared in Daana's Model Description Language, DMDL), and DAR (Data As Requirements needs it — metrics declared once with calculation, grain and dimensions). In every layer the declaration is the source of truth and SQL is a regenerated artifact; the acid test is whether your contract *generates* the unpacking logic or merely documents it. The post is explicit that this is not universally better — it names the cases where imperative code still wins and insists mature platforms carry both.

mandates.claim: DAS represents source systems without interpretation through two stages: landing zone and staging.
mandates.implication: DAS is not one layer but two physical stages. Ingestion writes a landing zone; a second, separate, contract-driven step produces staging. Do not collapse them into one dlt destination table.

mandates.claim: Landing receives raw data exactly as produced - often JSON strings with no schema enforcement. Staging unpacks to tabular format while remaining faithful to source structure.
mandates.implication: Land the payload as an unparsed JSON string column with no schema applied. Staging may reshape to columns but must not rename toward business concepts or apply business logic — it stays faithful to source structure.

mandates.claim: Ingestion is forgiving (accept all data as JSON); unpacking is strict (contract-driven).
mandates.implication: Two different validation postures in one layer: the ingestion step must never reject or drop a record for schema reasons; the unpacking step must enforce the contract's types and modes. Configure dlt for permissive/schema-less landing, not for schema evolution enforcement.

mandates.claim: Data is never lost when schemas change.
mandates.implication: An unknown or changed upstream field must still land. Schema drift is a contract-update event, not a pipeline failure.

mandates.claim: In declarative DAS, data contracts define unpacking. A 50-line YAML contract specifies source structure, target schema, and transformation rules. Systems generate 100+ lines of SQL to extract nested JSON fields, cast types, handle arrays, and create historized and latest views.
mandates.implication: The DAS generator must emit, per contract: nested JSON field extraction, type casts, array handling, and BOTH a historized view and a latest view. Latest/historized views are a DAS-layer deliverable, not only a DAB one.

mandates.claim: When sources change, you update the contract and regenerate SQL. Contracts are truth; SQL is artifact.
mandates.implication: Generated SQL must be disposable and never hand-edited. Any fix goes into the contract; regeneration must be idempotent and safe to re-run over existing output.

mandates.claim: If sources send incorrect data then corrections, "latest" views automatically reflect the corrected state.
mandates.implication: The latest view must be a late-arriving-correction-tolerant projection over the historized data (ordered by the source/event timestamp), not a snapshot or a first-write-wins table.

mandates.claim: The key distinction: is your contract documentation that someone manually keeps in sync with custom SQL, or does it directly generate unpacking logic? ... changing the contract changes the code, forcing accuracy.
mandates.implication: A contract that only annotates a hand-written model does not count. The build must wire the contract directly into codegen so the two cannot drift.

mandates.claim: You declare what a Subscription entity should be using Daana's Model Description Language (DMDL): entities with id/name/definition/description/attributes, and relationships with source_entity_id/target_entity_id.
mandates.implication: The DAB focal model input format is DMDL YAML with exactly two top-level collections shown — entities and relationships. Build the daana-cli input against these keys.

mandates.claim: From these declarations and a corresponding one for data mappings, systems generate transformation logic.
mandates.implication: DMDL entity/relationship files are NOT sufficient input. A second, separate data-mappings declaration is required — presumably binding DAB attributes to DAS staging columns. Two artifacts feed the DAB generator.

mandates.claim: They join source tables based on defined relationships, implement slowly changing dimension logic, and create both SUBSCRIPTION_HIST (complete history) and SUBSCRIPTION_LATEST (current state) views.
mandates.implication: Per entity, the DAB generator must emit exactly two objects following the <ENTITY>_HIST / <ENTITY>_LATEST naming pattern. Joins come from declared relationships — the modeler never writes a join. SCD handling is generator-owned, not hand-coded.

mandates.claim: Relationships need names, cardinalities, and clear definitions. Get them right and generated transformations correctly join data.
mandates.implication: Join correctness is entirely a function of the relationship declaration, so relationship modeling is the highest-risk activity in the build. Cardinality is stated as required even though the shown DMDL example carries no cardinality key.

mandates.claim: DAB's Account entity remains unchanged because it's defined in business concepts, not source fields. When a source system renames customerID to account_id, only DAS changes - you update the contract mapping.
mandates.implication: DAB attribute names must be business vocabulary, never source-column echoes. A source rename must be absorbable entirely inside the DAS contract mapping, with zero DMDL edits and zero DAR consumer impact — this is a testable invariant for the platform.

mandates.claim: You declare what entities should exist — their attributes, relationships, and rules — and transformations generate from those declarations.
mandates.implication: Rules are named as a third declarable component of an entity alongside attributes and relationships, so the DAB model format must accommodate them (no rules key appears in the shown DMDL example).

mandates.claim: DAR optimizes for actual usage - metrics, dimensions, aggregations, and serving patterns. Also declarative.
mandates.implication: DAR is scoped to consumption shapes only. It is declared, not hand-written — so a generated Unified Star Schema fits the post's intent, but the post specifies no star-schema structure itself.

mandates.claim: You declare the metric once: "MRR equals sum of monthly_value for active subscriptions, dimensioned by plan_type and region, grain of monthly." One declaration generates warehouse queries, drives API responses, and serves as documentation.
mandates.implication: A metric declaration must carry at minimum: calculation, filter/qualifier, grain, and dimensions — and must have three consumers (SQL generation, an API response path, and rendered documentation) from the one definition. Maintaining separate SQL per consumer is explicitly rejected.

mandates.claim: DAR optimizations shouldn't leak business logic.
mandates.implication: No business rules may be defined for the first time in DAR. Business semantics live in DAB; DAR only reshapes and aggregates them.

mandates.claim: Changes in DAS shouldn't cascade to DAB. DAB entities should be stable despite evolving sources. Separation requires discipline and design.
mandates.implication: Enforce the layer boundary structurally (separate directories/schemas/codegen passes), because the post says the separation only holds through discipline.

mandates.claim: Each layer is documented through its declarative definitions - structured enough for both humans and AI to navigate.
mandates.implication: Do not build a separate docs pipeline. Documentation must be a rendering of the same DMDL/contract/metric files that drive generation.

mandates.claim: The naming is deliberate: DAS/DAB/DAR foregrounds the purpose of each layer (what the data represents) rather than its position in a sequence or quality grade. They map to staging/core/marts in dbt terminology, or bronze/silver/gold in the medallion architecture.
mandates.implication: Use DAS/DAB/DAR as the literal naming in schemas and directories rather than bronze/silver/gold or staging/core/marts, since the naming choice is the point.

mandates.claim: Generated transformations follow established patterns consistently. Patterns encoded once, applied everywhere. Hundredth entity gets same error handling as the first.
mandates.implication: The generator must be pattern-uniform: every entity gets identical historization, incremental processing and error handling. Per-entity special-casing defeats the stated benefit.

mandates.claim: Platforms need model registries storing entity definitions as queryable metadata - not documentation sites, but active systems driving code generation.
mandates.implication: Entity definitions must be stored somewhere queryable and the generator must read from that store. A folder of YAML rendered to a static docs site does not satisfy this.

mandates.claim: And they need validation at the model level, catching errors before code generation rather than after deployment.
mandates.implication: Ship a model validator that runs before codegen (referential integrity of source_entity_id/target_entity_id, type vocabulary, mapping completeness), not just SQL tests after deploy.

mandates.claim: They need generation frameworks that reliably translate models into correct transformations while providing room for custom logic where standard patterns don't fit.
mandates.implication: An escape hatch for custom logic is required — but see the tradeoff table: 'Too many escape hatches undermine consistency.' The escape hatch must be deliberate and bounded.

mandates.claim: Debugging shifts too. Instead of stepping through SQL, you examine entity definitions, contract-source alignment, generation edge cases. Must understand both model definition AND generation logic.
mandates.implication: Generated SQL must remain readable and traceable back to the declaration that produced it, because debugging now spans model and generator.

mandates.claim: Testing means: Validate models: "Does this entity definition represent the business concept correctly?"
mandates.implication: Test suite targets the model layer (semantic correctness of entity definitions), not only generated SQL syntax and logic.

mandates.claim: Start with layers where patterns are clearest. Ingestion contracts often provide high return... Core business entities in the DAB layer offer similar benefits once you've established your domain model. Metrics definitions pay off when serving multiple consumption patterns.
mandates.implication: Build order is DAS contracts first, then DAB entities, then DAR metrics — and DAB is gated on having an established domain model.

mandates.claim: Build a few implementations, discover commonalities, then abstract. Premature abstraction before patterns emerge adds overhead without benefit.
mandates.implication: Do not design the generator against a hypothetical entity. Hand-build a few pipelines first, then generalize from what actually repeated.

mandates.claim: Upfront Investment (declarative): Weeks to months: framework setup, code generation tooling, team training.
mandates.implication: Budget weeks-to-months before the first generated pipeline pays off; this is not a days-scale start.

mandates.claim: Clear cases favor imperative approaches: one-off analyses, genuinely novel algorithms, performance-critical optimization, early-stage exploration, very small teams with simple needs (three sources, ten entities, one data engineer).
mandates.implication: Carve out an explicit imperative escape lane in the platform for these five cases, with documented guidance on when to use it — the post says mature platforms provide both.

mandates.claim: Domain teams don't get access to write arbitrary SQL against production tables. Instead, they declare domain models that platforms implement according to standards.
mandates.implication: Access model: domain teams get write access to model/contract files only. Central platform team owns patterns, standards, and the generation framework.

mandates.claim: Technical debt doesn't disappear - it shifts... you risk rigid abstractions that can't accommodate edge cases... you risk overly generic models lacking domain specificity.
mandates.implication: Two failure modes to actively mitigate in the build: over-rigid generators and under-specific entity models.

artifacts.name: DAS data contract (full YAML, verbatim)
artifacts.detail:
# Declarative approach: Data contract
version: "1.0"
valid_from: "2025-01-01"

endpoints:
  source:
    provider: kafka
    entity: user_events

schema:
  primary_keys:
    - user_id
    - event_id

  columns:
    - source_path: payload.userId
      target_name: user_id
      type: INTEGER
      mode: REQUIRED
      description: "User account identifier"

    - source_path: eventType
      target_name: event_type
      type: STRING
      mode: REQUIRED
      description: "Event type (USER_CREATED, USER_UPDATED, etc.)"

    - source_path: timestamp
      target_name: event_ts
      type: TIMESTAMP_MILLIS
      mode: REQUIRED
      description: "Event timestamp in milliseconds"

artifacts.name: version
artifacts.detail: version: "1.0" — quoted string. Contract version.

artifacts.name: valid_from
artifacts.detail: valid_from: "2025-01-01" — quoted ISO date. Implies contracts are time-versioned/effective-dated, supporting the post's point that contracts require 'thought about versioning, backward compatibility'.

artifacts.name: endpoints.source.provider
artifacts.detail: provider: kafka — unquoted. Names the source system type. Nested under endpoints: > source:. The 'endpoints' plural + named 'source' key implies other endpoint roles are possible.

artifacts.name: endpoints.source.entity
artifacts.detail: entity: user_events — unquoted. The source-side object/topic name.

artifacts.name: schema.primary_keys
artifacts.detail: A list of target-side column names: - user_id / - event_id. Composite keys supported. Note: event_id is listed as a primary key but is NOT declared in the columns list of the shown example.

artifacts.name: schema.columns[]
artifacts.detail: A list of column mappings, each with exactly five keys in this order: source_path, target_name, type, mode, description.

artifacts.name: source_path
artifacts.detail: Dot-delimited path into the source payload, unquoted. Examples: payload.userId (nested), eventType (top level), timestamp (top level). This is the mechanism for 'extract nested JSON fields'.

artifacts.name: target_name
artifacts.detail: Unquoted snake_case output column name. Examples: user_id, event_type, event_ts. Note the rename discipline: source camelCase (userId, eventType) becomes snake_case; 'timestamp' becomes 'event_ts'.

artifacts.name: type
artifacts.detail: Unquoted, SCREAMING_CASE. Observed values: INTEGER, STRING, TIMESTAMP_MILLIS.

artifacts.name: mode
artifacts.detail: Unquoted. Only observed value: REQUIRED. (BigQuery-style mode vocabulary; NULLABLE/REPEATED are not shown but implied by the naming convention.)

artifacts.name: description
artifacts.detail: Double-quoted free text. Used to carry enum vocabularies inline, e.g. "Event type (USER_CREATED, USER_UPDATED, etc.)".

artifacts.name: Contract type vocabulary
artifacts.detail: INTEGER, STRING, TIMESTAMP_MILLIS — the only DAS contract types shown. TIMESTAMP_MILLIS is notable: precision is encoded in the type name, not a separate key.

artifacts.name: DMDL
artifacts.detail: "Daana's Model Description Language (DMDL)" — the named YAML dialect for declaring DAB entities and relationships.

artifacts.name: entities[] keys
artifacts.detail: id, name, definition, description, attributes. All string values are double-quoted. definition and description are BOTH present and distinct: definition is the short gloss ("A customer subscription"), description is the fuller prose ("Represents an active or historical subscription to a service plan").

artifacts.name: attributes[] keys
artifacts.detail: id, name, definition, description (optional), type, effective_timestamp (optional), group (optional). description appears only on ACQUISITION_TYPE and STATUS; effective_timestamp is absent on SUBSCRIPTION_START_DATE and SUBSCRIPTION_END_DATE; type is absent on the grouped attribute MONTHLY_VALUE (type lives on the group members instead).

artifacts.name: effective_timestamp
artifacts.detail: Boolean, unquoted true/false. false on SUBSCRIPTION_ID (the key); true on ACQUISITION_TYPE, STATUS, MONTHLY_VALUE (the changing attributes). Omitted entirely on START_TIMESTAMP/END_TIMESTAMP-typed attributes. This is the flag that drives which attributes get slowly-changing-dimension treatment in the generated _HIST view.

artifacts.name: group
artifacts.detail: A list of sub-attributes composing one logical attribute. Used for a value+unit pair: MONTHLY_VALUE (type NUMBER) + MONTHLY_VALUE_CURRENCY (type UNIT). Group members carry id, name, definition, type. The parent carries effective_timestamp; the members do not.

artifacts.name: DMDL type vocabulary
artifacts.detail: Double-quoted, SCREAMING_CASE: "STRING", "NUMBER", "UNIT", "START_TIMESTAMP", "END_TIMESTAMP". Note these are semantic, not physical: START_TIMESTAMP/END_TIMESTAMP declare validity-interval roles rather than a datatype, and UNIT declares a unit-of-measure companion to a NUMBER.

artifacts.name: relationships[] keys
artifacts.detail: id, name, definition, source_entity_id, target_entity_id. All double-quoted. No cardinality key appears in the example even though the prose says relationships need cardinalities. Relationship ids read as verb phrases: BELONGS_TO_ACCOUNT, HAS_BASE_PLAN.

artifacts.name: id == name convention
artifacts.detail: In every entity, attribute, group member and relationship shown, id and name hold the identical string. Both are SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE and double-quoted.

artifacts.name: SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE identifiers
artifacts.detail: Entities: SUBSCRIPTION, ACCOUNT, BASE_PLAN. Attributes: SUBSCRIPTION_ID, ACQUISITION_TYPE, STATUS, SUBSCRIPTION_START_DATE, SUBSCRIPTION_END_DATE, MONTHLY_VALUE, MONTHLY_VALUE_CURRENCY. Attributes are prefixed with the entity name (SUBSCRIPTION_ID, SUBSCRIPTION_START_DATE) except for generic ones (STATUS, ACQUISITION_TYPE). Contrast with DAS, which uses lowercase snake_case (user_id, event_type, event_ts).

artifacts.name: SUBSCRIPTION_HIST / SUBSCRIPTION_LATEST
artifacts.detail: "create both SUBSCRIPTION_HIST (complete history) and SUBSCRIPTION_LATEST (current state) views" — pattern is <ENTITY_ID>_HIST and <ENTITY_ID>_LATEST. Two views generated per DAB entity.

artifacts.name: historized and latest views (DAS)
artifacts.detail: The DAS unpacking generator also creates "historized and latest views" — the same HIST/LATEST duality exists one layer down, at staging.

artifacts.name: DAS / DAB / DAR
artifacts.detail: DAS = "Data As System sees it"; DAB = "Data As Business sees it"; DAR = "Data As Requirements needs it". Explicit mapping: "they map to staging/core/marts in dbt terminology, or bronze/silver/gold in the medallion architecture."

artifacts.name: landing zone / staging
artifacts.detail: "DAS represents source systems without interpretation through two stages: landing zone and staging." Landing = raw as produced, often JSON strings, no schema enforcement. Staging = unpacked to tabular, faithful to source structure.

artifacts.name: Metric declaration shape (DAR)
artifacts.detail: Verbatim example: "MRR equals sum of monthly_value for active subscriptions, dimensioned by plan_type and region, grain of monthly." Components named across the post: calculation logic, grain, dimensions. Note the DAR example references monthly_value / plan_type / region in lowercase snake_case, not the DMDL SCREAMING_CASE.

artifacts.name: Three DAR outputs from one declaration
artifacts.detail: "One declaration generates warehouse queries, drives API responses, and serves as documentation." Elsewhere: "that declaration generates SQL for your warehouse, API responses for applications, and documentation for business users."

artifacts.name: data mappings declaration
artifacts.detail: "From these declarations and a corresponding one for data mappings, systems generate transformation logic." A second DAB-layer input file, named but never shown.

artifacts.name: Enum vocabularies (carried in description text)
artifacts.detail: ACQUISITION_TYPE: "Origin channel: ORGANIC, CAMPAIGN, REFERRAL, TRIAL_CONVERSION". STATUS: "Status derived from dates: ACTIVE, CANCELLED, EXPIRED". MONTHLY_VALUE_CURRENCY: "Currency code (USD, EUR, SEK)". Event types: "USER_CREATED, USER_UPDATED, etc.". All carried as prose inside description — there is no enum/allowed_values key.

artifacts.name: customerID -> account_id
artifacts.detail: "When a source system renames customerID to account_id, only DAS changes - you update the contract mapping. DAB's Account entity remains unchanged... DAR consumers are unaffected."

artifacts.name: 50-line YAML -> 100+ lines of SQL
artifacts.detail: Stated code-generation leverage for a single DAS contract.

artifacts.name: {{ ref() }}
artifacts.detail: dbt's model reference syntax, cited as the example of "improved imperative code, not declarative architecture" — "you write SQL - a SELECT statement referencing other models with {{ ref() }} syntax."

artifacts.name: Platform components required
artifacts.detail: Three named: (1) model registries storing entity definitions as queryable metadata; (2) generation frameworks that translate models into correct transformations while leaving room for custom logic; (3) validation at the model level, before code generation.

artifacts.name: Tools named in the post
artifacts.detail: Declarative/metrics: dbt semantic layer, Cube, Malloy, headless BI. Imperative/mature: dbt, Airflow, Fivetran. Source system in examples: Kafka (kafka-python KafkaConsumer, topic 'user_events', bootstrap_servers localhost:9092). NOT mentioned anywhere in the post: dlt, daana-cli, Unified Star Schema.

artifacts.name: Declarative vs imperative tradeoff table
artifacts.detail: Twelve rows, verbatim aspect names: Consistency, Quality, Documentation, Testing, AI Effectiveness, Productivity, Upfront Investment, Learning Curve, Edge Cases, Flexibility, Tooling Maturity, Debugging.

artifacts.name: Five cases where imperative wins
artifacts.detail: One-off analyses; Genuinely novel algorithms; Performance-critical optimization; Early-stage exploration; Very small teams with simple needs ("Three sources, ten entities, one data engineer").

quotes: Ingestion is forgiving (accept all data as JSON); unpacking is strict (contract-driven).
Contracts are truth; SQL is artifact.
DAS represents source systems without interpretation through two stages: landing zone and staging.
They join source tables based on defined relationships, implement slowly changing dimension logic, and create both SUBSCRIPTION_HIST (complete history) and SUBSCRIPTION_LATEST (current state) views.

Instead of writing SQL to calculate monthly recurring revenue in your BI tool, similar logic in your API, then documenting separately, you declare the metric once: "MRR equals sum of monthly_value for active subscriptions, dimensioned by plan_type and region, grain of monthly."
When a source system renames customerID to account_id, only DAS changes - you update the contract mapping.
Platforms need model registries storing entity definitions as queryable metadata - not documentation sites, but active systems driving code generation.
And they need validation at the model level, catching errors before code generation rather than after deployment.
openQuestions: The post explicitly poses the core modeling decisions as unresolved: "What is a 'subscription'? When does it begin - at signup, payment, or access grant? What makes it 'active'? These are business domain questions with technical implications." These must be decided per-domain before DMDL can be written.

The data-mappings declaration is named as a required second DAB input ("a corresponding one for data mappings") but its keys, file layout, and how it binds DAB attributes to DAS staging columns are never shown. This is the single biggest gap for anyone building the daana-cli DAB step.

Relationship cardinality: the prose says "Relationships need names, cardinalities, and clear definitions," but the DMDL relationships block has only id, name, definition, source_entity_id, target_entity_id — no cardinality key. How cardinality is expressed is undecided.
Entity "rules" are listed as a declarable component ("their attributes, relationships, and rules") but no rules key exists in the DMDL example. Where quality/business rules live is open.

STATUS is annotated "Status derived from dates: ACTIVE, CANCELLED, EXPIRED" — a derived attribute — but DMDL shows no expression/derivation key. Whether derivation is declared, generated from START_TIMESTAMP/END_TIMESTAMP, or hand-written is unspecified.

The exact SCD semantics of effective_timestamp: true/false are never spelled out, and the attributes typed START_TIMESTAMP / END_TIMESTAMP carry no effective_timestamp key at all. How the generator decides history granularity is left open.

The contract lists primary_keys: user_id, event_id but event_id has no corresponding columns entry. Whether primary_keys must resolve to declared target_name values (and what validation enforces it) is unstated.

Enum vocabularies (ORGANIC/CAMPAIGN/REFERRAL/TRIAL_CONVERSION, ACTIVE/CANCELLED/EXPIRED, USD/EUR/SEK) are carried as prose inside description strings. Whether allowed values should become a first-class key is an open design choice.

DAR's physical shape is entirely unspecified. The post names metrics, dimensions, aggregations and serving patterns but gives no YAML, no schema, and never mentions a Unified Star Schema. The USS choice is not sanctioned or constrained by this post.

Escape hatches: the platform must provide "room for custom logic where standard patterns don't fit," yet "too many escape hatches undermine consistency." Where the line sits is explicitly left to the builder.

Contract evolution: the post says contract design "requir[es] thought about versioning, backward compatibility, and error handling at the contract level," but only shows version and valid_from. The versioning scheme is a decision to make.
The model registry's storage/query technology is unspecified — only that entity definitions must be "queryable metadata" driving generation, not a docs site.
Whether DMDL entity ids are globally unique or namespaced per domain is unaddressed, despite the post advocating federated ownership where "domain teams own their models."
dlt and daana-cli are never mentioned in the post; the post does not constrain the ingestion tool beyond requiring forgiving, schema-less landing, so the dlt configuration choice is unguided here.

result.title: AI-Assisted Data Engineering: A Practical Methodology
result.thesis: AI fails at real data engineering not because of model capability but because of an information gap: it lacks business domain knowledge, architectural knowledge, data contracts, and process knowledge for your platform. The fix is architectural — make the platform declarative so metadata IS the implementation (YAML definitions that generate transformation code, contracts that drive testing, conventions agents can consume), and extend that structure across the whole platform rather than only the semantic/analytics last mile. On top of that structure, each of the three layers (DAS / DAB / DAR — Data As System, Data As Business, Data As Requirements) demands a fundamentally different AI interaction pattern, served by specialized agents with rigid workflows rather than one general assistant. The architecture dictates how AI participates, not the other way around.

mandates.claim: The layers are named DAS, DAB, DAR — Data As System, Data As Business, Data As Requirements — deliberately instead of Bronze/Silver/Gold, 'because the names encode what the data represents at each layer, not just its position in a pipeline.'
mandates.implication: Name the layers and their artifacts by what the data represents (system / business / requirements), not by pipeline position. The layer name is itself carrying semantics that humans and agents read; do not alias back to medallion terminology.

mandates.claim: 'That semantic clarity matters: it tells both humans and AI agents what kind of work belongs where.' Layer boundaries 'become semantic checkpoints.'
mandates.implication: Layer separation must be explicit and enforceable — a checkpoint an agent can test against, not a convention. Work must be refusable at the wrong layer.

mandates.claim: DAS is the staging layer and its mandate is 'Translation fidelity: raw source data to clean, typed, well-documented staging tables.'
mandates.implication: DAS output must be typed and documented at the column level. Fidelity to source is the only success criterion; nothing derived belongs here.

mandates.claim: 'YAML data contracts define the rules. The agent works within them. The constraints are features: you can't accidentally inject business logic into pure staging.'
mandates.implication: The DAS contract format must be structurally incapable of expressing business logic. The prohibition is enforced by the contract schema, not by reviewer discipline.

mandates.claim: 'Each contract specifies a single source-to-staging transformation: which raw table to read, what fields to extract, how to type-cast them, what expected values look like.'
mandates.implication: One contract = one source table → one staging table. Four required content areas per contract: source table reference, field selection, type-cast rules, expected-value specification. Expected values are part of the contract, not a separate test file.

mandates.claim: 'A Python generator reads these contracts and produces SQLX files that Dataform executes against BigQuery.'
mandates.implication: Staging SQL is generated, never hand-written. The contract is the editable artifact; the SQL is build output.

mandates.claim: 'What makes this powerful for AI is the constraint, not the automation. The contract specifies what staging must produce. When the agent encounters a new source system — Kafka event streams, MySQL CDC data, MongoDB collections, BigQuery cross-project tables — the template tells it exactly what to verify and how.'
mandates.implication: There must be a contract template that carries per-source-system verification instructions, so a new source type is onboarded by filling a template rather than by improvising. The value delivered is the constraint surface, not the code savings.

mandates.claim: 'A 4-tier testing framework validates every contract's output: syntax validation through dry-run compilation, NULL detection across millions of records, and automatic root cause analysis for extraction errors.'
mandates.implication: Every contract's output is validated — no opt-out. At minimum: dry-run compile, NULL detection at full row scale (not sampled), and automated root-cause analysis for extraction errors. (The fourth tier is not named in the post.)

mandates.claim: 'Historical data alignment is where AI assistance provides the most leverage - and fails most instructively. Source systems don't follow the same conventions across eras: column names change, value encodings shift, fields captured now were never captured historically. The staging agent treats every historical alignment as a potential trap - always querying actual data distributions before assuming compatibility, never trusting naming consistency.'
mandates.implication: Historical alignment needs a distinct, defensive workflow in DAS: query actual value distributions before unioning eras; never infer compatibility from matching column names.

mandates.claim: 'In the staging layer - DAS - AI works as a reader and investigator.'
mandates.implication: DAS agent capabilities should be read/profile-heavy: query distributions, read schemas and descriptions. Generation is templated; investigation is the actual work.

mandates.claim: 'In the business layer - DAB - AI works as a builder and debugger. Source data becomes business entities: subscriptions with acquisition types, orders with payment levels, campaigns with attribution categories. The work shifts to derivation and investigation - expressing business concepts as transformation expressions, testing edge cases against real data, tracing anomalies back through layers.'
mandates.implication: DAB is where business entities are formed and where derivation lives. The DAB unit of work is a transformation expression attached to a business concept, plus edge-case tests against real data, plus cross-layer traceability so an anomaly can be traced back to DAS/source.

mandates.claim: An `Information Modelling Agent` 'drafts information models for new business domains by researching the company, decomposing business questions into constituent measures and dimensions, and generating structured model definitions. It works before any data flows - turning stakeholder conversations into formal entity definitions that downstream agents consume. Its output becomes the shared vocabulary every other agent references.'
mandates.implication: The information/focal model is authored BEFORE ingestion, from business questions decomposed into measures and dimensions, and is emitted as structured model definitions. It is the single shared vocabulary every other layer and agent dereferences — so it must be a machine-readable file, not prose.

mandates.claim: 'Your semantic model becomes a shared language between humans and AI.'
mandates.implication: The semantic/business model is the human-AI interface artifact; it must be readable and re-readable at any point by any agent.

mandates.claim: 'In the reporting layer - DAR - AI works as a designer and analyst. Dimensional modeling: defining proper grain, building conformed dimensions, ensuring additive measures, verifying point-in-time correctness.'
mandates.implication: DAR carries four explicit correctness obligations: declared grain, conformed dimensions, additive measures, and point-in-time correctness. Each needs to be checkable, not asserted.

mandates.claim: A `Kimball Agent` 'builds the consumption layer - dimensions, facts, snapshots - carrying a mandatory 5-test protocol it refuses to skip.'
mandates.implication: DAR object types are dimensions, facts, and snapshots. A fixed test protocol must run on every DAR object and must be non-skippable by construction.

mandates.claim: Grain and per-key nullability are stated as human-supplied inputs to the DAR agent: 'This is factless_fact_order with grain (order_key, fact_ts). base_plan_key can be NULL before activation. offer_key can be NULL when no campaign applies.'
mandates.implication: Every fact table declaration must carry an explicit grain tuple and per-column nullability semantics with the business reason for the NULL. Then the agent verifies grain across the full table (4.4 million rows in the example) and profiles NULLs across every column.

mandates.claim: 'What's new is making metadata executable and machine-readable: YAML definitions that generate transformation code, contracts that drive testing, conventions in formats AI agents can consume. A DevOps-inspired approach where metadata IS the implementation - documentation can't drift because it's the same artifact as the code.'
mandates.implication: Three separable requirements: (1) YAML definitions generate transformation code; (2) contracts drive test generation; (3) conventions are stored in an agent-consumable format. No second documentation artifact may exist alongside the metadata.

mandates.claim: 'If you're building data platforms today, the highest-leverage investment isn't AI tooling. It's making your platform declarative. Semantic models with clear definitions. Data contracts specifying transformations and constraints. Documented conventions. Explicit layer separation.'
mandates.implication: Four required platform components, in priority order over any agent tooling: semantic models, data contracts (transformations + constraints), documented conventions, explicit layer separation.

mandates.claim: 'Verify before you generate.' / 'Now "understand the architecture first" is encoded in every agent's workflow. Before writing SQL, check INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMN_FIELD_PATHS for column descriptions. Read the view definitions. Understand what's upstream.'
mandates.implication: Architecture-first is a workflow step encoded in every agent, not advice. Three concrete pre-generation reads: warehouse column descriptions via INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMN_FIELD_PATHS, view definitions, and upstream lineage. This implies column descriptions must actually be populated in the warehouse for the platform to be agent-legible.

mandates.claim: 'one AI agent against all tasks produces mediocre results... an agent that knew a little about everything and was expert at nothing. It confused layer responsibilities, mixed transformation patterns, and occasionally applied business rules from one entity to another entirely. The breakthrough came from specialization. Distinct agents, each with a focused role and clear boundaries.'
mandates.implication: Build one agent per layer/role with hard boundaries, plus an orchestration layer that delegates and maintains context — not a single system prompt covering the platform. The named failure modes of the general agent (layer confusion, pattern mixing, cross-entity business rule leakage) are the boundaries the specialists must enforce.

mandates.claim: 'A multi-group mapping bug exposed the problem. The agent spent four iterations patching symptoms before we forced a stop and traced the full architecture: YAML contracts fed a compiler producing JSON, which fed a calculation engine generating SQL for BigQuery. The bug wasn't in the mapping expression. It was in how the compiler handled multi-group joins... The answer was a targeted architectural workaround, not a sequence of band-aids.'
mandates.implication: The compile chain (YAML → JSON IR → SQL generator) is itself a debugging surface. Bugs surfacing as bad mapping values may live in the compiler's join handling, so the IR must be inspectable and agents must be able to reason about the whole chain rather than only the expression they authored.

mandates.claim: 'Declarative architecture pays off here: an agent that "forgets" mid-session can re-align by reading the semantic model, contracts, and column descriptions.'
mandates.implication: The platform must be re-readable as a recovery mechanism: semantic model + contracts + column descriptions together must be sufficient to fully re-orient an agent with zero conversation history. Nothing load-bearing may live only in chat.

mandates.claim: Named failure modes: 'Patching without understanding', 'Context window limits', 'Overconfidence in SQL - queries passing syntax checks but embedding subtle logic errors (counter: validation against known test cases)', 'Moving too fast - changing code without branching, assuming columns exist without querying, mapping from names rather than data.'
mandates.implication: Four guardrails to build in: root-cause-before-fix, architecture re-read on context loss, validation against known test cases (syntax passing is not correctness), and a mandatory branch workflow with column-existence queries and data-based (not name-based) mapping.

mandates.claim: 'Humans provide what AI can't: domain knowledge, intent, judgment, and investigative direction... AI provides what humans struggle with under time pressure: systematic investigation of every column and value distribution, pattern recognition across thousands of records, mechanical accuracy in repetitive SQL, and tireless validation against every constraint.'
mandates.implication: Design the workflow so humans supply business rules, grain, nullability semantics, and direction; agents supply exhaustive column-by-column profiling and constraint validation over every row. Do not ask agents for judgment or spot-check humans into validation work.

mandates.claim: 'Once caught, these mistakes get permanently internalized... Systematic retrospectives with agents - reviewing decisions, encoding corrections into workflows - turn individual fixes into durable process improvements.'
mandates.implication: Corrections must be written back into agent workflows/conventions as a routine step, so a fix applies to every subsequent mapping rather than only the current session.

mandates.claim: 'If you want a Monday morning starting point, begin with testing. Write down how your team validates a new table or transformation today - grain checks, NULL analysis, foreign key integrity, edge cases. Hand that checklist and warehouse access to an AI agent... You don't need a declarative platform to start - you need one process, documented clearly enough for an agent to follow.'
mandates.implication: The first deliverable is a written validation checklist (grain, NULL, FK integrity, edge cases) executed exhaustively over every row — build the declarative platform around that, not before it.

mandates.claim: 'The industry has partially figured this out - for the last mile. Semantic layers and metric stores (Cube, Omni, dbt's MetricFlow) work precisely because they give AI structured business context for querying... But what about the 90% of data engineering before analytics?'
mandates.implication: Do not stop at a consumption-layer semantic model. The same structured-context treatment must be applied to staging, business logic derivation, dimensional modeling, testing, and validation.
