result.title: The Work Before the Answer
result.thesis: A narrative case study of Nextory (Nordic audiobook streaming) rebuilding its data platform with Daana. The argument: the blocker to trustworthy AI-over-data was not technology but clarity — even the leadership team held different definitions of the same entities — so the fix was to make definitions the implementation rather than documentation that drifts. Concretely, the platform ingests source data raw as a big JSON blob (no schema commitment at ingestion), and a per-source data contract owned by the data-producing product team declares how that blob is unpacked; the staging SQL is auto-generated by scripts reading those contracts, so every staging table behaves identically across sources. The author also confesses a sequencing mistake — building DAS in full depth-first cost ~six weeks and hid a silent identifier collision — and prescribes building the entire stack thin first.

mandates.claim: Ingestion must not commit to a schema. The old platform "ingested data into structured tables (i.e. we had committed to a schema during ingestion), which always created issues when source schema changed"; the new platform ingests "the data raw from source with everything in a big JSON blob."
mandates.implication: Configure dlt to land the source payload raw — a single JSON/blob column per record — rather than letting it infer, normalize, or enforce a structured relational schema at load time. Source schema change must not break ingestion.

mandates.claim: There is one data contract per source, and it is "owned by the data producing product team." The contract "lists how this raw data should be unpacked into a structured format."
mandates.implication: The contract is a per-source declarative artifact carrying an explicit producing-team owner. Model ownership as a first-class field, and scope one contract file per source system, not per table or per pipeline.

mandates.claim: The structured tables are not hand-written: "The actual SQL that produces the structured tables with unpacked data is then auto-generated by scripts that read each contract and applies the contract rules to build the SQL."
mandates.implication: Staging/unpacking SQL is build output, not checked-in source to be edited. You maintain the contract; the SQL is its mechanical consequence. Any hand-edit of generated SQL is a defect in the contract or the generator.

mandates.claim: Uniformity across sources is the point: "we instead focus just on the data contract, and can feel confident that every staging table will work exactly the same across all sources." The old platform's failure was per-source drift in "naming conventions, rules about what logical steps that were allowed in the staging layer, and overall query structure."
mandates.implication: The generator must enforce one canonical staging shape: identical naming convention, identical set of permitted logical steps, identical query structure. Per-source special-casing is the anti-pattern being eliminated — no escape hatch for 'this source is different'.

mandates.claim: "At Nextory, definitions and implementations are not two different things... Nextory built a platform where the definition is the implementation. The platform reads those definitions and turns them into the running system. Change a definition, change the system."
mandates.implication: No second copy of definitions in a wiki, Confluence page, or data catalog. The definition artifacts the business argues about must be the same files the generator consumes; there must be no documentation surface that can drift from the code.

mandates.claim: Generation must not produce a black box. Xiaoyan Zhang's objection was resolved by observing that "The business logic is still fully visible, the transformations are still there, you just don't need to write the boilerplate code."
mandates.implication: Generated output must be readable, inspectable artifacts where business logic and transformations remain legible — only boilerplate is removed. Debuggability and absence of vendor opacity are acceptance criteria, not nice-to-haves.

mandates.claim: Depth-first layer construction was a mistake: "We built the DAS layer... first, in full, before we had anything end-to-end." The corrective: "What I'd do differently is build the entire stack thin first. A skeleton at every layer that someone can look at, even if it's wrong. Then iterate against existing trusted reports where possible. Depth comes after the loop closes."
mandates.implication: Build a thin vertical slice through DAS, DAB and DAR before deepening any one layer. Validate against pre-existing trusted reports. The stated cost of getting this wrong was about six weeks.

mandates.claim: Depth-first ordering hid a real defect: "a silent identifier collision I didn't find until I started building a thin DAR prototype... Two records that should have been distinct were being merged into one because of how I'd composed the identifier. The bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it."
mandates.implication: Composed identifiers/business keys are a known silent-failure surface. Need distinctness/collision assertions on composed identifiers in DAS, and an end-to-end consumption view early enough to expose merges that DAS-local tests will not catch.

mandates.claim: The entity definitions are "the formal, written-down names for the things the business actually runs on, customers and subscriptions and content and territories" — and they "weren't a deliverable for the wiki. They were the actual model the platform runs on."
mandates.implication: The business/focal model input is a written entity definition set, presented to and contested by leadership. The named example entities are customers, subscriptions, content, territories. Leadership disagreement on a definition should resolve into a code change.

mandates.claim: "By coupling an enriched data model and a semantic layer with MCP capabilities, we enabled the entire organisation to get trusted answers." The CEO "connected Claude to Nextory's data via MCP and asked the question in plain English."
mandates.implication: The serving layer is exposed as an enriched data model plus a semantic layer, reachable over MCP by an agent. The semantic layer is what makes the natural-language conversation reproducible across the organization rather than a one-person trick.

mandates.claim: "SQL is no longer a requirement to use the warehouse directly." The prior state was "governance by obscurity" — stakeholders "were shut out from doing more complex analysis without a data team member being part of the analysis and reviewing the work."
mandates.implication: The consumption layer must be safe for non-SQL stakeholders operating through agents without a data-team reviewer in the loop. Reviewing agent output does not scale; the structure itself must make the analysis defensible.

mandates.claim: "Agents benefit greatly from clear structure, good naming and clear context (this is in my experience often even more important than exactly which LLM model you pick)." Also: "I'm quite sure that the agents would write worse SQL in our old platform, while also spending more tokens on trial and error to end up with queries that actually work."
mandates.implication: Naming and structural consistency in the generated models are functional requirements with measurable agent-behavior consequences (SQL quality, token spend on trial and error) — not cosmetic style choices.

mandates.claim: "when everyone works from the same definitions, production systems start converging to map against the business logic, not the other way around." The post calls this the inversion of dependency direction, contrasted with platforms that "inherit the structure of the systems that produced the data" and retrofit business logic on top.
mandates.implication: The business layer must not be shaped by source-system structure. The business definitions are fixed and sources map toward them, which means the DAB model is authored from business entities, not derived from what the source schema happens to expose.

mandates.claim: Xiaoyan raised a concentration concern that the post reports but does not resolve: "if the generation step is load-bearing for the whole platform, you've concentrated the platform's maintenance into whoever owns that step."
mandates.implication: Treat the generator as a single point of maintenance concentration and plan for it (ownership, readability, bus factor). The post offers visibility of generated logic as partial mitigation, not a full answer.

mandates.claim: Planned next layer: "a knowledge layer that keeps track of our full platform, with a lineage graph of all assets and how they connect, enriched with human-curated structured context covering architecture, rules, gotchas and everything an agent will need in order to understand how to use the data." It "would have been much more complex to build this knowledge layer in our old platform, if even at all possible."
mandates.implication: Design DAS/DAB/DAR so asset-level lineage is derivable and so human-curated context (architecture, rules, gotchas) can attach to assets. This is stated as future work at Nextory, not something already built.

mandates.claim: Organizational placement is treated as a design decision: the data role "sat under the COO, not under IT." "Data is a business concern that happens to run on technology."
mandates.implication: Ownership of the platform belongs to the business side. The post frames putting data under IT as optimizing the measurable part and starving the part that matters.

mandates.claim: The data contract is described as the organizational unit of accountability, not merely a technical file: "The contract isn't just a technical artifact. It's the unit of accountability." This is what produced "clearer data ownership."
mandates.implication: Contract authorship/review must sit with the producing product team as a governance mechanism; the file's owner is who gets held accountable for the source's structure.

mandates.claim: Declarative work shifts effort upstream rather than removing it: "Changes that used to take days now take hours" because in the old platform "time was spent remembering" per-source conventions.
mandates.implication: Expect the cost model to move to contract/definition authoring done once and reused, and expect team discussion to move to architecture-general rather than source-specific topics.

quotes: In the old platform, we ingested data into structured tables (i.e. we had committed to a schema during ingestion), which always created issues when source schema changed.
We ingest the data raw from source with everything in a big JSON blob.
Then we have a data contract for each source, owned by the data producing product team, that lists how this raw data should be unpacked into a structured format.
The actual SQL that produces the structured tables with unpacked data is then auto-generated by scripts that read each contract and applies the contract rules to build the SQL.
In the new platform we instead focus just on the data contract, and can feel confident that every staging table will work exactly the same across all sources.
The business logic is still fully visible, the transformations are still there, you just don't need to write the boilerplate code.
What I'd do differently is build the entire stack thin first.

Agents benefit greatly from clear structure, good naming and clear context (this is in my experience often even more important than exactly which LLM model you pick), and this is exactly what you get in a declarative framework.
openQuestions: The post never names or defines DAB. It defines DAS ("ingestion, raw-to-structured, representing the system perspective of the data") and DAR ("consumption/serving layer of the data") verbatim, but the business layer appears only obliquely as "entity definitions," "enriched data model" and "semantic layer." Where the focal model lives relative to those three names is not settled here.

None of the tools the builder intends to use are mentioned anywhere in the post: dlt, daana-cli, and Unified Star Schema do not appear. Daana is named once ("This is the reason Daana exists"). Any mapping from these principles to those tools is the builder's inference, not the post's instruction.

The data contract's concrete form is unspecified — no file format, no YAML/JSON keys, no directory layout, no schema for the contract itself, and no example. The post says only that it "lists how this raw data should be unpacked into a structured format" and that scripts "read each contract and applies the contract rules."

No table or column naming rules, SQL constructs, or type mappings are given anywhere, even though "good naming" and identical "naming conventions" across sources are stated as requirements. The specific convention must be chosen by the builder.

Identifier composition is left open: a bad composition caused a silent merge of two records that should have been distinct, but the post does not say how identifiers should be composed, nor what test would have caught it earlier beyond looking at the data end-to-end.

Schema evolution is only half-answered: raw JSON-blob ingestion removes the ingest-time break, but what happens to the contract, the generated SQL, and downstream models when the source schema changes is not described.

Xiaoyan's concentration concern is raised and left unresolved: "if the generation step is load-bearing for the whole platform, you've concentrated the platform's maintenance into whoever owns that step." The post answers only her opacity objection, not this one.
"Then iterate against existing trusted reports where possible" — the hedge "where possible" leaves open what to validate a thin stack against when no trusted report exists.

How the semantic layer is exposed over MCP is unspecified: no tool surface, granularity, permissioning, or server design. Likewise how "trusted answers" are made verifiable for stakeholders working without a data-team reviewer.
Contract ownership by "the data producing product team" is stated as a principle; how it is enforced, reviewed, or approved (PR process, CODEOWNERS, sign-off) is not described.
The knowledge layer (lineage graph plus human-curated context on architecture, rules and gotchas) is explicitly future work — its structure, storage, and how agents consume it are entirely open.

result.title: Context Isn't Enough: Agentic Analytics Eventually Has to Fix the Data
result.thesis: Teams are improving analytics agents by layering context around the data — skills, semantic layers, rules files, and now formal ontologies (OSI, Microsoft Fabric IQ) — and it demonstrably works (Anthropic: 21% → ~95%; Claire Gouze: 4% → 82%). But every such layer is a map over a platform it did not shape: it goes stale, costs tokens on every question, crowds out other context, and remains advice rather than an enforced rule, so residual failures come from the data model itself (bad joins on shared primary keys, unfiltered nulls, business rules living in people's heads, metrics requiring model changes). The post argues the durable fix is to declare the business model — entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules turning source data into analytical facts — and let a compiler generate the physical platform, so naming, identifiers, historization, grain, validation and documentation are built in rather than documented on top. The declared model becomes the ontology and the warehouse becomes its output; a semantic layer can be exposed from the same declarations instead of maintained beside them. This is presented as the idea behind Daana (YAML business models compiled into deployed transformation infrastructure).

mandates.claim: "Define the business model declaratively: entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules that turn source data into analytical facts. Then let a compiler generate the physical implementation."
mandates.implication: The DAB focal model is the ONLY hand-authored surface, and it must be able to express all seven of those element kinds. Physical DDL, transformations and pipeline code are compiler output — a builder writes model declarations, not SQL files.

mandates.claim: "The declared model is the source and the warehouse is an output."
mandates.implication: The warehouse is regenerable and disposable. No hand-edits to deployed objects; any change starts in the declaration and is re-compiled. Round-tripping fixes back from the warehouse into the model is excluded.

mandates.claim: "Naming is uniform because it is generated."
mandates.implication: Table/column naming must be produced by the generator from the model, not by team convention or hand-written style guides. Naming rules live in the compiler; no per-source or per-team naming dialects survive into DAS/DAB/DAR.

mandates.claim: "Every entity gets identifiers from the start."
mandates.implication: Identifier declaration is mandatory, not retrofitted. An entity with no declared identity should not be a legal model — this forecloses the "keys are missing or loosely defined" failure the post lists.

mandates.claim: "Historization is something you declare, with one mechanism everywhere, rather than something each pipeline solves in its own way."
mandates.implication: One single historization mechanism across the whole platform, selected by declaration per entity/source. Rules out a mix of historized tables and overwrite-in-place tables where "nothing tells you which" — so per-pipeline load-strategy choices (including at the ingestion tool level) must be driven by the model, not configured independently.

mandates.claim: "Grain is fixed per entity"
mandates.implication: Grain is a declared property of an entity, enforced by the compiler. Mixed-grain tables must be structurally impossible rather than documented as a gotcha.

mandates.claim: "attributes are modeled as answers to atomic business questions: a loan amount is not just a number, but a number plus a currency"
mandates.implication: Attributes carry their full semantic payload (value + unit/currency) as one modeled thing. A bare numeric column is an under-specified attribute; the attribute type system must support composite, unit-bearing values.

mandates.claim: "Logic is defined once and compiled wherever it is needed"
mandates.implication: A rule is authored in exactly one place and fanned out by the compiler into every layer that needs it. Re-implementing the same logic in DAS, DAB and DAR (the post's "same logic implemented three times with three subtly different results") is the failure mode being designed out.

mandates.claim: "nothing deployed can be orphaned, because everything derives from the current model"
mandates.implication: Deployment is a complete projection of the current model: objects not derived from it are removed or reconciled. No orphaned pipelines or leftover tables from previous model versions.

mandates.claim: "A semantic layer can be exposed from the same declarations rather than maintained on the side."
mandates.implication: The requirements/serving layer (and any semantic layer or star schema) is generated from the DAB declarations. Maintaining a parallel semantic-layer definition is precisely the drift the post warns about.

mandates.claim: "In effect, the model becomes the ontology, except the platform is generated from it instead of merely described by it."
mandates.implication: Do not build a separate ontology artifact over the platform. If ontology-shaped output is needed (concepts, typed relationships, identity declarations, constraints, derivation rules), emit it from the model.

mandates.claim: "with identifiers, historization, naming consistency, validation, and documentation generated rather than hand-maintained" (Daana: "business models defined in YAML, compiled into deployed transformation infrastructure")
mandates.implication: Five specific outputs must be generator responsibilities, not human ones: identifiers, historization, naming consistency, validation, documentation. The authoring format named is YAML; the compile target is deployed transformation infrastructure.

mandates.claim: "A rule the agent has to remember is weaker than a rule the platform enforces."
mandates.implication: Whenever a constraint is expressible in the model, express it there instead of in agent instructions/skills/rules files. Agent-facing prose is the last resort, not the first.

mandates.claim: "Context can route an agent to the right answer only if the platform contains a right answer to route to." / "If forty plausible revenue datasets exist underneath, the semantic layer can route around the confusion, but it has not made the confusion disappear."
mandates.implication: Resolve duplicate and near-duplicate definitions in the model rather than routing around them downstream. A single business decision must have one representation, not one each in the warehouse, semantic layer, docs and agent instructions.

mandates.claim: Compensating documentation "goes stale" (Anthropic's accuracy fell "from roughly 95% to 65% within a month"), "is also expensive, since every gotcha means more tokens for the agent to read on every question", "crowds out other context", "and in the end it is advice rather than a rule."
mandates.implication: Do not budget a growing "gotchas" document as the fix for platform ambiguity; each of the four costs (staleness, tokens, crowd-out, non-enforcement) applies. If any hand-maintained context remains, the post names what it took to stop the rot: colocated docs, CI hooks, automated correction harvesting.

mandates.claim: "None of this solves everything. A generated platform still inherits the quality of its source systems, and a poorly chosen model compiles just as reliably as a good one."
mandates.implication: Generation guarantees consistency, not correctness. Source-data quality (the DAS input) and modeling judgment (the DAB design) still need human review and governance — the compiler will not catch a bad model.

mandates.claim: "the description and the implementation can no longer drift apart, because one is produced from the other"
mandates.implication: Non-drift is the design goal to preserve: any feature that lets documentation, semantic definitions or agent context be edited independently of the model reintroduces the problem the architecture exists to remove.

mandates.claim: "a generated platform is legible by construction: an agent that learns the shape of one entity knows the shape of all of them"
mandates.implication: Uniformity across entities is an agent-facing feature, not cosmetics. Per-entity special cases, escape hatches and bespoke overrides erode the property that makes the platform navigable.

mandates.claim: Anthropic's stack "uses skills to help the agent retrieve and follow the right context, but the foundation is still the governed data underneath: canonical datasets, deprecated near-duplicates, enforced standards, maintained metadata, freshness checks, and validation."
mandates.implication: Even a generated platform needs the governance list named here — canonical designation, explicit deprecation of near-duplicates, enforced standards, metadata, freshness checks, validation. Generation does not remove the need for these; it changes where they are declared.

mandates.claim: "For Anthropic, the hard part is mapping a user's question to the right entities in the data model; once that works, writing the SQL is easy."
mandates.implication: Optimize the serving layer for question-to-entity mapping (unambiguous, well-identified entities), not for SQL generation ergonomics. SQL generation is not the bottleneck being solved.

openQuestions: Which single historization mechanism? The post mandates "one mechanism everywhere" but never names it (no SCD type, no validity-interval scheme, no bitemporal-vs-unitemporal choice).

What form does the generated semantic layer take? The post says it "can be exposed from the same declarations" but does not say in what format or against which interface — OSI, dbt, Fabric IQ, or a star schema are all left open.

Whether to emit or interoperate with the OSI ontology specification (concepts, typed relationships, identity declarations, constraints, derivation rules). The post says "the model becomes the ontology" but does not say whether the model should serialize to OSI or ignore it.
How is model quality reviewed? "A poorly chosen model compiles just as reliably as a good one" identifies the gap but proposes no review process, linting, or modeling methodology to close it.

How the governance list (canonical datasets, deprecated near-duplicates, enforced standards, maintained metadata, freshness checks, validation) is expressed in a declarative model — the post says the foundation is still governed data, but not which of those become YAML declarations versus separate process.

What generation cannot fix at the source boundary: "a generated platform still inherits the quality of its source systems" — the post gives no guidance on where source-quality handling (nulls, loose keys, missing history) lives relative to the declared model.

What context is still worth writing over a generated platform. "Context that explains a well-structured platform is leverage" — but the post never says what that residual context contains, how much, or where it lives.
The general attribute type system beyond the loan-amount-plus-currency illustration: which atomic business questions get first-class composite types is not specified.

How the mandates map onto a three-layer DAS/DAB/DAR split — the post argues at the level of "the model" and "the platform" and never names layers, so the placement of identifiers, historization and grain across the three layers is a builder decision.
How to migrate an existing messy platform. The post's advice is "stop building mazes" but it offers no path from the existing estate to the generated one beyond the Nextory case study reference.

result.title: Designing for Agentic Experience: Why AX is the New UX
result.thesis: Most AI interactions fail not because models are weak but because our systems, docs and processes were built for humans and rely on unstated shared context — the author calls this the "sticky-note problem." The fix is to design deliberately for "Agentic Experience" (AX): systems with clear semantic definitions, explicit rules and boundaries, and documented processes instead of tribal knowledge. The author gives a sequential methodology (think manually → translate to explicit steps → walk one example slowly → have the AI write the process for another LLM → retrospect and refine → eventually specialize and delegate) and frames delegation as progressive trust rather than day-one autonomy. It is a working-methodology post, not an architecture post: it names no data layers, no schemas, and no commands.

mandates.claim: "Clear semantic definitions" are the first requirement of an agent-friendly system: "Humans can work with ambiguous terminology because we intuit from context. Agents can't." The example given is documentation saying "the service handles user data" — an agent cannot tell whether that means authentication, profile information, or behavioral tracking.
mandates.implication: Every named entity/measure/attribute must carry an unambiguous written definition rather than a name an agent is expected to intuit; a bare model or column name is not a definition.

mandates.claim: "Explicit rules and boundaries" are the second requirement: "We often leave rules implicit because humans 'just know' them. An agent needs those rules stated directly. What's allowed? What's forbidden? What requires approval?"
mandates.implication: Rules the platform enforces (naming, allowed transformations, what an agent may change unattended vs. what needs sign-off) must be written down as stated rules, including an explicit approval boundary — not left to convention.

mandates.claim: "Documented processes, not tribal knowledge" is the third requirement; the named failure mode is knowledge living in people's heads ("Oh, you need to run that by Sarah first." "We always format dates that way because of the legacy system.").
mandates.implication: Any operating procedure (how a source gets onboarded, why a field is shaped a certain way) must exist as a document an agent can read, and the reasons behind conventions must be recorded, not just the conventions.

mandates.claim: Agent-friendliness aligns with good architecture specifically through declarativeness: "When you declare what you want rather than prescribing how to do it, both humans and agents can navigate the system more effectively."
mandates.implication: Prefer declarative specification of intent (what the model/output should be) over imperative step-by-step code, since the post claims declarative systems are the ones both humans and agents can navigate.

mandates.claim: The methodology begins before any AI is involved: "Before you involve AI at all, think through how you would do the task yourself. Not in vague terms - actually walk through it." "If you can't articulate the task precisely for yourself, you certainly can't articulate it for an agent."
mandates.implication: Do not start an agent-automated build step by prompting; first write out by hand what the step checks, what patterns it looks for, and how it decides a violation from an acceptable edge case.

mandates.claim: Step two is to write the process out as actual steps and then have a real conversation with the AI about it — "Here's what I'm trying to accomplish. Here are the steps I think are involved. What am I missing?" — because "The AI often spots gaps in your thinking - assumptions you made implicitly, edge cases you didn't consider."
mandates.implication: Treat the explicit written process as a reviewable draft to be interrogated by the model for missing edge cases before it is automated.

mandates.claim: Step three is a single slow, confirmed end-to-end example: "The AI explains what it's about to do before doing it. You confirm or correct each step." "premature speed creates compounding errors."
mandates.implication: Before generating anything at scale (e.g. across many sources or models), run one instance with explain-before-act and per-step human confirmation; scaling out before that walk-through is the named failure mode.

mandates.claim: Step four produces the agent's documentation: "ask the AI to describe the process 'in its own words, suitable for another LLM to follow.' This becomes your agent's 'way of working' document." The post insists "The phrasing matters."
mandates.implication: Agent-facing process docs should be generated by the model after a successful walk-through using that exact framing, not hand-written as human-facing docs, because the framing captures implicit context that surfaced during the walk-through.

mandates.claim: Step five is a retrospective after each real use: "What went wrong? What assumptions turned out to be incorrect? Update the process document. Refine the prompts." The author keeps "a simple log: what worked, what didn't, what to change."
mandates.implication: Ship a change log alongside the process document recording why each constraint was added, so constraints remain explicable on later iterations.

mandates.claim: Specialization comes last and only after stabilization: "Once a process has stabilized through several iterations, you can create a specialized agent with its own focused context. It works more independently, only coming back to you when it hits something outside its defined boundaries."
mandates.implication: Specialized/autonomous agents are an outcome of several stabilized iterations, not a starting configuration, and each must have defined boundaries that trigger escalation to a human.

mandates.claim: The steps are strictly sequential: "You can't document for the agent until you've walked through an example. You can't walk through an example until you've translated your thinking into explicit steps."
mandates.implication: Do not skip ahead in the ladder; each artifact is the precondition for the next.

mandates.claim: Delegation is progressive, not blind: "You start with tight oversight and frequent corrections. You graduate to documented processes with spot checks. Eventually you reach a point where specialized agents work independently and you review outcomes rather than steps." Handing AI complex judgment-heavy tasks on day one is named as "a common mistake."
mandates.implication: Autonomy level is a staged setting (oversight → documented process + spot checks → outcome review), and the first automated tasks should be mundane and low-stakes, not the hardest ones.

mandates.claim: The round-table technique requires a specific kind of environment: "it requires an environment where you can store documentation, reference it across sessions, and spin up specialized agents. AI-enabled IDEs (Cursor, Windsurf), agentic CLI tools (Claude Code, Gemini CLI), or similar. Standard chat interfaces don't support this workflow."
mandates.implication: The tooling must support persistent stored documentation, cross-session reference to it, and spawning multiple specialized agents; a plain chat UI is explicitly ruled out.

mandates.claim: Agents should do mechanical verification and escalate ambiguity: "You shouldn't spend hours manually checking naming conventions when an agent can do the mechanical verification and surface only the ambiguous cases for your decision." "The goal throughout is not to replace human judgment."
mandates.implication: Automated checks should partition into deterministic pass/fail handled by the agent and an explicit ambiguous-case queue routed to a human.

mandates.claim: Start with one mundane, repetitive task — "documentation formatting, boilerplate generation, code review checklist verification" — because "the methodology itself is what you're learning"; starting with "refactor our entire authentication system" means learning methodology and domain complexity simultaneously.
mandates.implication: Pick a low-stakes repetitive step of the build as the first agentic workflow; applying only the first three steps is explicitly endorsed ("You don't have to build a production-ready workflow on day one.").

result.title: Stop Being the Naming Convention Police
result.thesis: Naming conventions fail not because people are careless but because enforcement is disconnected from the documentation: the style guide lives in Confluence/Notion while the code lives in the IDE, and traditional linters force you to maintain a second, machine-readable copy of the rules that inevitably drifts. The post proposes making the documentation itself executable: on every pull request, CI/CD spawns an AI agent (e.g. via Claude Code CLI) that uses MCP to fetch the live convention document, comprehends it rather than regex-matching it, and posts violations with the cited rule, a suggested fix, and a severity. Because the agent comprehends context, it can enforce rules that regex cannot express ("names should reflect business concepts, not technical implementation") and can recognize legitimate exceptions, e.g. a forbidden word appearing in a source-table column you do not control. Rollout guidance: start with one convention, run warning-only for a week or two, clarify the doc to fix false positives, then block only on critical violations.

mandates.claim: The post's worked example convention: "metrics should follow the pattern `<descriptor>_<entity>_<unit>`, with entities in plural form and without words like 'total' or 'sum' (because scope is handled elsewhere in the semantic layer)." It is presented as an illustrative convention, not as the author's universal law.
mandates.implication: If you adopt this shape for the generated Unified Star Schema / metric layer, measure names get built as descriptor + plural entity + unit (orders_count, revenue_amount) and the generator must never emit total_/sum_ prefixes; aggregation scope is expressed through filters in the semantic layer, not encoded into the name.

mandates.claim: "The AI agent reads your documentation that says 'scope words like total and sum should not appear in metric names because the semantic layer handles aggregation scope through filters.'" The rule exists because scope is a filter concern.
mandates.implication: The DAR/USS layer must own aggregation scope via filter context; a metric name is a stable identity, so a naming rule banning scope words is only coherent if the semantic layer actually provides scope through filters.

mandates.claim: Naming rules require context: "Is `total_orders` wrong because it uses a forbidden word, or is it acceptable because it's a column in a source table you don't control? A regex can't make that distinction."
mandates.implication: Convention enforcement must be scoped by layer. Columns landed from a source system (the DAS layer, which you do not control) are a legitimate exception to naming rules; only names you author (DAB/DAR) are subject to them. Any review step you build must be able to tell the two apart, which is exactly what a pure regex linter cannot do.

mandates.claim: "Documentation is enforcement. The same artifact serves both purposes." Do not maintain two versions of the conventions - "the human-readable one that people actually consult, and the machine-readable one that enforces rules" - because "These two inevitably drift apart."
mandates.implication: Do not translate the platform's naming standards into a separate linter config or ruleset file. Keep one natural-language convention document as the source of truth and have the enforcement agent read that document at review time, so updating the doc immediately changes enforcement with no sync step.

mandates.claim: The enforcement flow is: a developer commits code and opens a pull request; CI/CD triggers a specialized AI agent (via something like Claude Code CLI); the agent uses MCP to fetch the naming convention from your documentation platform; it analyzes the changed files against the fetched rules; the agent posts a review with any violations found, suggested fixes, and explanations; optionally, it can auto-fix simple violations and create a fix commit.
mandates.implication: Build convention review as a PR-triggered CI job that runs an agent with MCP access to the docs platform, operating on the changed files only. Auto-fix-and-commit is explicitly optional, not required.

mandates.claim: Agent output must be more than pass/fail: each finding names the offending line and identifier, the issue, the standard it violates (quoted from your doc), a suggested fix, and a severity. "The feedback isn't just 'error on line 3.'"
mandates.implication: The review output format is fixed by the post's example: VIOLATION / Line N / Issue / Standard / Suggested fix / Severity. The stated payoff is that "The developer learns something, and they're much more likely to remember the convention next time."

mandates.claim: "The agent can also assign severity levels. A metric name that breaks a semantic layer contract might be critical and block the PR. A style preference violation might be minor and just generate a warning." Also: "treating them all as blocking errors creates friction that makes people resent the system."
mandates.implication: Severity must be graded, and the blocking threshold tied to whether a semantic-layer contract is broken. Do not make every convention violation a build failure.

mandates.claim: "Fourth, and this is important, run in warning-only mode first. Don't block PRs immediately. Let the system run for a week or two and see what it catches."
mandates.implication: Ship convention enforcement in non-blocking mode first, observe for one to two weeks, and only then "turn on blocking for critical violations and keep warnings for lesser issues."

mandates.claim: False positives are fixed by editing the documentation, not by adding exceptions to a tool: "Maybe your documentation isn't as clear as you thought and the agent is catching things you didn't intend. Maybe there are false positives you need to address by clarifying your conventions." The calibration period "will help to make your document clearer, like for instance distinguishing between hard rules and guidelines."
mandates.implication: Your convention document needs an explicit hard-rule vs guideline distinction, and the remediation loop for bad agent findings is a doc edit - never a divergent tool config.

mandates.claim: "Start with one convention, prove the value, and grow from there." "For most data teams, metric naming is a good starting point because it's high impact and the rules tend to be clear." Otherwise, "write up the one that causes you the most pain."
mandates.implication: Do not attempt to encode the platform's whole style corpus up front. Begin with metric naming, then expand to other conventions (e.g. a SQL style guide) once it demonstrably works.

mandates.claim: The agent can enforce conventions that are impossible to express as regex: "Rules like 'metric names should be self-explanatory without requiring documentation lookup' or 'names should reflect business concepts, not technical implementation' are easy for humans to understand but nightmarish to encode as pattern matching."
mandates.implication: Business-facing naming rules (business concepts over technical implementation, self-explanatory without a doc lookup) are enforceable and belong in the convention document - they are exactly the kind of rule the DAB focal-model naming needs and that a regex-based check would have to drop.

mandates.claim: "I'm a firm believer in metadata-driven data engineering-the idea that 'harder' metadata like data contracts and entity definitions can be used to make sure documentation and implementation are aligned. However, what I was still struggling with was 'softer' things like naming conventions and style guides."
mandates.implication: Two-tier alignment strategy: hard metadata (data contracts, entity definitions) enforces structure mechanically; soft conventions (naming, SQL style) are enforced by the doc-reading agent. The agent approach complements contracts and entity definitions rather than replacing them.

mandates.claim: "set up MCP configuration in your CI environment. There are existing MCP servers for Atlassian, Notion, and other platforms. The configuration is straightforward, mostly a matter of providing API credentials and pointing to the right server."
mandates.implication: CI needs an MCP config file plus API credentials for the docs platform; the post names Atlassian (Confluence), Notion, GitHub and Slack as available MCP servers and links a Notion example config.

mandates.claim: The agent needs "a focused prompt" of the shape: "Fetch page X from Notion. Review the changed files in this PR against the conventions described in that page. Report any violations with explanations and suggested fixes."
mandates.implication: The prompt is a versioned repo artifact (prompts/review-conventions.md in the example repo) naming the specific doc page, the diff scope, and the required output content.

result.title: Why We Built Daana: Reclaiming Lost Knowledge
result.thesis: A founder-origin manifesto (Siavoush Mohammadi, April 27 2026) arguing that the "big data" era discarded decades of data-modeling discipline — Kimball, Inmon, ensemble modeling — leaving teams with brittle hand-written SQL, medallion layers that mean nothing, and architectural knowledge trapped in a few senior heads. The fix is not more books but encoding the patterns into tooling: declare business entities, attributes and relationships in YAML, and let the system generate transformation pipelines that follow a three-layer architecture (DAS / DAB / DAR) where each layer name encodes purpose rather than position. The post's second half is a concrete demo of that: a focal-model YAML shape, two `daana-cli` commands, three generated views per entity, and a time-travel query against generated history. The semantic model is deliberately the single source that humans read, LLMs read, and transformation generation consumes, so the three cannot drift apart.

mandates.claim: The three layers are named for purpose, not position: "Data As System sees it, Data As Business sees it, Data As Requirements needs it", and the post explicitly equates them to staging/core/marts and bronze/silver/gold while rejecting the ambiguity of the latter ("ask three people what belongs in silver and you'll get four answers").
mandates.implication: Use DAS/DAB/DAR as the actual layer names in schemas, directories and docs. Each layer must have a stateable membership rule that three people would answer identically; do not carry bronze/silver/gold naming forward.

mandates.claim: "Source changes stay isolated in DAS."
mandates.implication: DAS is the containment boundary for upstream schema drift. Nothing downstream may reference a source column shape directly; a source-side change must terminate in DAS and be absorbed by the DAS→DAB mapping, not ripple into DAB or DAR.

mandates.claim: The post names "the same late discovery that mixing source representation with business logic makes everything unmaintainable" as one of the repeated failures being solved.
mandates.implication: DAS holds source representation only. No business rules, no conformance, no semantics in the ingestion layer.

mandates.claim: "The three-layer architecture enables practical patterns like forgiving ingestion and self-healing pipelines" (details deferred to 'The Rise of the Model-Driven Data Engineer').
mandates.implication: Ingestion is expected to tolerate malformed/changed input rather than fail hard; the architecture is the precondition for that. The post does not specify the mechanism here.

mandates.claim: "When you need to capture how the business actually works - handling source systems that change underneath you while preserving historical context - that's where ensemble modeling techniques earn their keep in the Data As Business (DAB) layer."
mandates.implication: DAB is an ensemble-modeled layer whose two jobs are absorbing source change and preserving history. Do not build DAB dimensionally.

mandates.claim: "Business semantics stabilize in DAB."
mandates.implication: DAB is the stability contract for everything downstream. DAR consumers bind to DAB entity semantics, and DAB entity/attribute identifiers should change far less often than either source schemas or report requirements.

mandates.claim: The DAB model is declared as YAML entities with `id`, `name`, `definition`, and `attributes` (each with `id`, `definition`, `type`, `effective_timestamp`), plus named `relationships` carrying `name`, `definition`, `source_entity_id`, `target_entity_id`.
mandates.implication: The focal model file is the DAB source of truth and its shape is fixed. Every attribute must carry a human-readable `definition` — the definition is not optional commentary, it is what LLMs and readers consume.

mandates.claim: "These relationships drive join logic in the generated views. You don't write the joins - the model does."
mandates.implication: Joins must never be hand-authored. If a join is needed, the missing thing is a declared relationship, not a SQL file. Relationships are declared with business verb names (IS_FOR_PRODUCT, BELONGS_TO), not as FK constraints.

mandates.claim: "You map these entities to source tables - which columns feed which attributes, how to handle timestamps, how to merge data from multiple sources."
mandates.implication: A source-mapping artifact sits between DAS and DAB and is a distinct concern from the entity model: column→attribute feeds, timestamp handling, and multi-source merge rules all live there. The post does not show its file format.

mandates.claim: Daana generates exactly three views per entity: current state, full history, and current state with relationships joined.
mandates.implication: The DAB→DAR interface is these three views per entity. Build DAR against VIEW_<ENTITY>, VIEW_<ENTITY>_HIST and VIEW_<ENTITY>_WITH_REL; do not read DAB physical tables underneath them.

mandates.claim: "No historization code written. No SCD2 logic. No temporal join patterns. The entity definition drives everything."
mandates.implication: Hand-written SCD2, effective-dating, or as-of join code in the platform is a defect — it means something belongs in the entity definition and was not declared there.

mandates.claim: "The history built itself from your entity definition and source mappings."
mandates.implication: History is a derived property of declaration (attributes marked `effective_timestamp: true` plus the source mapping), not a pipeline someone maintains.

mandates.claim: "When you're shaping data for how people actually analyze it, dimensional modeling remains the natural choice for the Data As Requirements (DAR) layer."
mandates.implication: DAR is dimensional. (The post says dimensional modeling generally and does not name Unified Star Schema.)

mandates.claim: "Consumption patterns in DAR evolve without touching upstream layers."
mandates.implication: Adding, changing or dropping a DAR consumption model must require zero edits to DAB or DAS. If a new report forces an upstream change, the layering has been violated.

mandates.claim: "Normalized models fit operational reporting. Event-driven patterns handle real-time needs." — modeling technique is chosen per purpose, not globally.
mandates.implication: DAR may hold more than one shape; dimensional is the default for analysis, but operational reporting and real-time needs get their own patterns rather than being forced into the star.

mandates.claim: "Your semantic definitions serve triple duty: what you read to understand the business model, what LLMs read when answering questions about your data, and what drives transformation generation. These aren't three separate artifacts that can drift - they're the same source."
mandates.implication: One YAML model, three consumers. No separate data dictionary, no separate LLM context file, no separate transformation spec. Any design that produces a second describing-artifact is wrong.

mandates.claim: "Update the model, transformations regenerate automatically." and "Hundreds of hand-written SQL models maintaining transformation logic become generated artifacts of a semantic model that you design and evolve."
mandates.implication: Generated SQL/views are build output, not source. They must be regenerable from scratch and must never be hand-edited or reviewed as the unit of change — the model file is the reviewed unit.

mandates.claim: "Declare what you want - business entities, relationships, semantic meaning - and let the system generate how to build it following sound architectural principles. Documentation becomes implementation."
mandates.implication: Work order is declare → generate. The design step produces YAML, not SQL. Confluence-style parallel documentation is explicitly the failure mode being eliminated.

mandates.claim: Deployment is two commands: `daana-cli deploy` and `daana-cli execute`.
mandates.implication: Treat deploy (materialize the generated objects) and execute (run the load) as separate steps in CI/CD and orchestration; the post shows no other CLI verbs.

mandates.claim: "There are trade-offs. Learning declarative modeling requires shifting from imperative SQL thinking. You gain consistency but sacrifice some flexibility in custom transformations. The generated output may not match exactly what you'd hand-build."
mandates.implication: Do not scope the build assuming byte-for-byte parity with existing hand-written SQL, and expect cases the declarative model cannot express. The post does not describe an escape hatch.

mandates.claim: "The repetitive, pattern-following work that consumed most of the engineering effort gets automated. What remains is the work that actually requires human judgment: understanding the business, modeling semantics correctly, and making architectural decisions."
mandates.implication: Staff and time-budget the project around semantic modeling sessions with the business, not around SQL authoring. Effort estimates based on model counts are the wrong unit.

mandates.claim: "It works on BigQuery, Snowflake, and other cloud platforms."
mandates.implication: Warehouse portability is assumed; avoid engine-specific constructs in anything hand-written around the generated layer.

mandates.claim: "This is alpha because we're still learning. The core patterns work - we've used them across organizations with consistent results. But translating those into a tool that works for diverse teams requires feedback from people building real systems under real constraints."
mandates.implication: daana-cli is alpha software. Expect gaps and interface churn; the architectural patterns are the stable part, the tool is not.

mandates.claim: "We deliver this by working directly with teams - building their platforms alongside them, transferring knowledge as we go."
mandates.implication: The intended adoption mode is co-build with the vendor, not self-serve from docs alone.

artifacts.name: entities:
artifacts.detail:
Top-level YAML key holding a list of entity definitions. Verbatim first block:
entities:
  - id: "CUSTOMER"
    name: "CUSTOMER"
    definition: "Customer who places orders"
    attributes:
      - id: "CUSTOMER_NAME"
        definition: "Full name of the customer"
        type: "STRING"
        effective_timestamp: true

artifacts.name: id / name / definition / attributes
artifacts.detail: The four entity-level keys shown. `id` and `name` are identical in both examples ("CUSTOMER"/"CUSTOMER", "ORDER_LINE"/"ORDER_LINE"). `definition` is prose: "Customer who places orders", "Individual item within an order".

artifacts.name: id / definition / type / effective_timestamp
artifacts.detail: The four attribute-level keys shown. Every attribute in both examples sets `effective_timestamp: true` (unquoted boolean).

artifacts.name: type: "STRING" / type: "NUMBER"
artifacts.detail: The only two attribute types appearing in the post. Uppercase, double-quoted. STRING used for names, cities, statuses and identifiers (ORDER_LINE_ID); NUMBER used for QUANTITY and LINE_AMOUNT.

artifacts.name: relationships:
artifacts.detail:
Top-level YAML key, shown at the same indentation level as `entities:` (column 0) in the second block. Verbatim:
relationships:
  - name: "IS_FOR_PRODUCT"
    definition: "Line item references a product"
    source_entity_id: "ORDER_LINE"
    target_entity_id: "PRODUCT"

  - name: "BELONGS_TO"
    definition: "Order line belongs to an order"
    source_entity_id: "ORDER_LINE"
    target_entity_id: "ORDER"

artifacts.name: name / definition / source_entity_id / target_entity_id
artifacts.detail: The four relationship keys. Note relationships use `name` (not `id`) as their identifier, unlike entities and attributes which use `id`.

artifacts.name: IS_FOR_PRODUCT, BELONGS_TO
artifacts.detail: Relationship names are business verb phrases in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, read source→target: "an order line IS_FOR a product and BELONGS_TO an order". IS_FOR_PRODUCT embeds the target noun; BELONGS_TO does not — both forms appear.

artifacts.name: CUSTOMER, ORDER, ORDER_LINE, PRODUCT
artifacts.detail: Entity ids/names are singular, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE nouns. Four entities appear across the examples.

artifacts.name: CUSTOMER_NAME, CUSTOMER_CITY, CUSTOMER_STATUS, ORDER_LINE_ID, QUANTITY, LINE_AMOUNT
artifacts.detail: Attribute ids are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Descriptive attributes of an entity are prefixed with the entity name (CUSTOMER_NAME, CUSTOMER_CITY, CUSTOMER_STATUS, ORDER_LINE_ID); measures on ORDER_LINE are not prefixed (QUANTITY, LINE_AMOUNT).

artifacts.name: daana-cli deploy
artifacts.detail: First of the "two commands" run after entities are defined and mapped to source tables. No flags shown in the post.

artifacts.name: daana-cli execute
artifacts.detail: Second of the two commands. No flags shown in the post.

artifacts.name: VIEW_CUSTOMER
artifacts.detail: "Current state. One row per customer, latest attribute values." One of three views generated per entity.

artifacts.name: VIEW_CUSTOMER_HIST
artifacts.detail: "Full history. Every change tracked, time-travel ready."

artifacts.name: VIEW_CUSTOMER_WITH_REL
artifacts.detail: "Current state with relationships already joined." The relationship declarations are what drive these joins.

artifacts.name: VIEW_<ENTITY> / VIEW_<ENTITY>_HIST / VIEW_<ENTITY>_WITH_REL
artifacts.detail: Inferred pattern from the three named CUSTOMER views: "Daana generates transformation logic and creates three views per entity in your data warehouse". Prose writes them uppercase; the SQL example references them lowercase (view_customer_hist).

artifacts.name: daana_dw
artifacts.detail: The warehouse schema qualifying generated views in the example: FROM daana_dw.view_customer_hist

artifacts.name: eff_tmstp
artifacts.detail: Physical effective-timestamp column on the history view, produced by attributes declared `effective_timestamp: true`. Used for both filtering (eff_tmstp <= '2024-11-27') and ordering (ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC). Values are dates in the sample output: 2024-11-05.

artifacts.name: customer_key
artifacts.detail: Entity key column on the generated view, pattern <entity>_key. Compared to a quoted string literal in the example: WHERE customer_key = '2'. No key/business-key declaration for it appears in the shown YAML.

artifacts.name: customer_name, customer_city, customer_state
artifacts.detail: Physical columns in the generated view are the lowercase form of the YAML attribute ids. Note customer_state is selected although no CUSTOMER_STATE attribute appears in the YAML excerpt (the excerpt is partial).

artifacts.name: Point-in-time query pattern
artifacts.detail:
Verbatim:
-- Where was this customer living on November 27th?
SELECT customer_name, customer_city, customer_state, eff_tmstp
FROM daana_dw.view_customer_hist
WHERE customer_key = '2'
  AND eff_tmstp <= '2024-11-27'
ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC
LIMIT 1;

The as-of idiom is: filter the _HIST view by key, bound eff_tmstp <= <as-of date>, ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC, LIMIT 1.

artifacts.name: Sample result row
artifacts.detail:
Verbatim:
customer_name | customer_city | customer_state | eff_tmstp
Emily Johnson | Boston        | MA             | 2024-11-05

Scenario: "a customer moved from Boston to Philadelphia on November 29th" — changing the date to November 29th returns Philadelphia.

Source changes stay isolated in DAS. Business semantics stabilize in DAB. Consumption patterns in DAR evolve without touching upstream layers.

When you need to capture how the business actually works - handling source systems that change underneath you while preserving historical context - that's where ensemble modeling techniques earn their keep in the Data As Business (DAB) layer. When you're shaping data for how people actually analyze it, dimensional modeling remains the natural choice for the Data As Requirements (DAR) layer.

You map these entities to source tables - which columns feed which attributes, how to handle timestamps, how to merge data from multiple sources. Then you run two commands: daana-cli deploy and daana-cli execute.
No historization code written. No SCD2 logic. No temporal join patterns. The entity definition drives everything.

openQuestions: The post never mentions Unified Star Schema. DAR is specified only as "dimensional modeling" — whether USS, classic Kimball stars, or something else fills DAR, and how the three generated DAB views feed it, is entirely unaddressed here.
The post never mentions dlt or any ingestion tool. How DAS is populated, and how DAS tables are handed to daana-cli, is left open.

The source-to-entity mapping artifact is described in prose ("which columns feed which attributes, how to handle timestamps, how to merge data from multiple sources") but no file, YAML keys, or format is shown. Its shape must be decided from the docs, not this post.

Which ensemble technique actually generates DAB is not named. Hultgren and Linstedt are cited as influences, but whether the generated layer is Data Vault (hub/link/sat), Ensemble/Focal, or a proprietary variant is not stated.

Whether `entities:` and `relationships:` are sibling top-level keys in one file or live in separate files is ambiguous — the second code block starts mid-list at entity indentation and then drops `relationships:` to column 0.
Entity `id` and `name` are identical in both examples ("CUSTOMER"/"CUSTOMER"). Whether they may legitimately differ, and what each is used for downstream, is not explained.

Key declaration is unspecified: the generated view exposes `customer_key` and the query filters on it, but nothing in the shown YAML declares a business key, natural key, or key-generation rule. Composite keys are explicitly deferred to the tutorial.
`effective_timestamp: true` appears on every attribute in both examples. Whether it is required, what `false` produces, and whether non-historized attributes are supported is not stated.
Multi-source merging is named as a capability but deferred: "For a full walkthrough covering multi-source merging, composite keys, and more complex modeling patterns, see the Daana tutorial."

The two shown commands (`deploy`, `execute`) cover generating and running DAB. Nothing in the post says how or whether DAR/mart generation is triggered, or whether it is in scope for daana-cli at all.

Attribute case: YAML ids are uppercase (CUSTOMER_NAME) and physical columns are lowercase (customer_name); whether this is a defined lowercasing rule or warehouse-dependent identifier folding is not stated.

The example SQL selects `customer_state`, but no CUSTOMER_STATE attribute appears in the CUSTOMER YAML block — the YAML excerpt is partial, so the full required attribute set for the demo is not recoverable from the post.

The escape hatch for transformations the declarative model cannot express is acknowledged ("sacrifice some flexibility in custom transformations") but never described. Whether custom SQL can be injected, and where, is open.

Daana's relationship to dbt — replace, sit on top of, or complement — is explicitly deferred to "The Rise of the Model-Driven Data Engineer", as is the guidance on "when declarative makes sense and when to stay imperative".
"Forgiving ingestion" and "self-healing pipelines" are asserted as enabled by the architecture but their mechanics are deferred to the same sibling post.
Data contracts appear in the tags and in one passing sentence, with no statement of where contracts sit relative to DAS/DAB/DAR or how they are declared.

result.title: Meet Peiman Khorramshahi: CTO at Daana
result.thesis: A personal-background interview with Peiman Khorramshahi, Daana's CTO, framed around the thread connecting satellite FPGA/ASIC design, agile coaching, and data platforms: they are all "complex systems." The only build-relevant content is incidental: daana-cli was architected and built from the ground up in Go, converting what had previously been Patrik's pure SQL-based Focal framework into "a proper engineering platform"; its hardest architectural decision was separation of concerns; it ships with a new automated test harness; and it is deliberately skewed so the user surface is very simple while the engine carries the complexity. It contains no description of the DAS/DAB/DAR layering, no mention of dlt, and no mention of the Unified Star Schema.

mandates.claim: "Peiman architected and built daana-cli from the ground up in Go, turning what was previously Patrik's pure SQL-based Focal framework into a proper engineering platform."
mandates.implication: daana-cli is a Go program, not a SQL macro library or a Python framework. A builder integrates with it as a compiled binary invoked as a CLI, and should expect the Focal model logic that used to live in hand-written SQL to now be owned and emitted by that engine rather than maintained as SQL by hand.

mandates.claim: The Focal framework it replaced was "pure SQL-based" and belonged to Patrik; daana-cli makes it "a proper engineering platform."
mandates.implication: The DAB focal model has a pre-existing pure-SQL lineage. Treat daana-cli as the engineered successor to that SQL framework — i.e. the focal model is the thing daana-cli exists to produce — but note the post gives no focal-model syntax, keys, or table rules to implement against.

mandates.claim: "Separation of concerns was the hardest. To make sure each part was doing its own thing and not cluttered with everything."
mandates.implication: The single stated architectural principle of the tool: each component does one thing and is not cluttered with the rest. A three-layer build should keep the layers' concerns in genuinely separate components rather than letting one stage reach into another.

mandates.claim: "Another thing that is worth mentioning was the brand new automated test harness to make sure every feature we deliver behaves like what we promise."
mandates.implication: An automated test harness that asserts each feature behaves as promised is treated as a first-class deliverable alongside the engine itself — build it as part of the platform, not after it. It is named again at the end of the post as validating "everything" in v0.7.0.

mandates.claim: "I think the balance is OFF by a lot meaning the user now has a VERY easy way of doing very complex things done by the engine."
mandates.implication: The declarative-simplicity vs. engine-complexity tradeoff is deliberately and heavily skewed toward the user. Complexity belongs inside the engine; the user-facing surface must stay simple and declarative even when that costs engine complexity.

mandates.claim: "A CLI tool that can quickly turn the wheels is invaluable. Especially because it can be used by both humans and AIs."
mandates.implication: The CLI surface is intended to be driven by AI agents as well as humans, so command and output design must be agent-consumable, not just human-ergonomic.

mandates.claim: The v0.7.0 release of daana-cli "brings incremental batch loads, parallel pipeline execution, and a bunch of architectural improvements."
mandates.implication: Incremental batch loading and parallel execution of pipelines are capabilities of the tool as of v0.7.0 — an ingestion/loading design should assume batch-incremental (not purely full-refresh) loads and pipelines that can run concurrently. The post gives no configuration detail for either.

mandates.claim: "I see data platforms as a means to an end when it comes to getting insight on anything that matters to you. It speeds up the process of creating robust systems with minimum waste."
mandates.implication: Stated design intent: the platform exists to shorten the feedback loop to insight, which argues for prioritizing time-to-first-insight over platform completeness. This is a philosophy statement, not a technical constraint.

artifacts.name: Why We Built Daana: Reclaiming Lost Knowledge

artifacts.name: From Business Question to Working Prototype in Hours
artifacts.detail: Named as the next article in the blog series — the title suggests it covers the requirements-to-DAR path this post does not.

quotes: Peiman architected and built daana-cli from the ground up in Go, turning what was previously Patrik's pure SQL-based Focal framework into a proper engineering platform.
Separation of concerns was the hardest. To make sure each part was doing its own thing and not cluttered with everything.
Another thing that is worth mentioning was the brand new automated test harness to make sure every feature we deliver behaves like what we promise.
Well it depends on what you mean. I think the balance is OFF by a lot meaning the user now has a VERY easy way of doing very complex things done by the engine.
A CLI tool that can quickly turn the wheels is invaluable. Especially because it can be used by both humans and AIs.

Peiman is currently heads-down on the v0.7.0 release of daana-cli - the platform he architected and built from scratch - which brings incremental batch loads, parallel pipeline execution, and a bunch of architectural improvements.
I think it is possible to create fully autonomous agents that can build your whole stack with super high quality just by asking the business people questions.
I see data platforms as a means to an end when it comes to getting insight on anything that matters to you. It speeds up the process of creating robust systems with minimum waste.
openQuestions: The post never names the DAS / DAB / DAR layers, dlt, or the Unified Star Schema. Anyone building that three-layer architecture gets no layer definitions, boundaries, or contracts from this post — those must come from elsewhere in the blog (the linked 'Why We Built Daana: Reclaiming Lost Knowledge' and 'From Business Question to Working Prototype in Hours' are the obvious candidates).

'Separation of concerns' is named as the hardest and most important architectural decision, but the post never says what the concerns actually are or where daana-cli draws the boundaries. Whether the separation follows the DAS/DAB/DAR seams, or some orthogonal decomposition, is left open.
No daana-cli command, subcommand, flag, config file name, or YAML key appears in the post. The entire CLI surface for producing the DAB focal model is unspecified here.

'Incremental batch loads' is named as a v0.7.0 capability but its mechanism is unstated — whether incrementality is cursor-based, high-watermark, CDC, or delegated to the ingestion tool, and how it is configured, is left open. The relationship (if any) between daana-cli's loading and dlt is never mentioned.
'Parallel pipeline execution' is named but the unit of parallelism, dependency resolution between pipelines, and any concurrency limits are unspecified.

The automated test harness is stated to validate 'that every feature behaves like what we promise' and 'validates everything', but what it asserts against — generated SQL, loaded data, model shape — and how a builder writes tests in it is not described.

The user surface is stated to be deliberately 'VERY easy' and declarative while the engine carries the complexity, but no example of that declarative input is shown, so the actual authoring format is left open.

The claim that 'fully autonomous agents ... can build your whole stack ... just by asking the business people questions' is offered as a hot take about what is possible, not as a description of how daana-cli works today — whether any of that question-asking flow is implemented is left open.

result.title: Meet Lars Fredholm: Principal Data Engineer at Daana
result.thesis: An interview-format team introduction to Lars Fredholm (investor-turned-builder at Daana, previously Head of Data at Advisa and at Validio). His argument: data modeling has been forgotten because modern cheap, decoupled storage and compute removed the short-term punishment for doing it badly, and tools/patterns like dbt and Medallion actively loosen modeling discipline — producing an unmaintainable mess about a year in. Daana's answer is automated, metadata-driven data modeling that starts from real-world business logic, producing an unambiguous model that both ingest (upstream) and metrics/BI (downstream) become a function of. He argues unambiguity is now a hard requirement because AI needs unambiguous input to produce reliable output, and warns against copying software-engineering modularity (microservices) wholesale into the data stack.

mandates.claim: Data modeling must be metadata-driven and must start from the actual real-world (aka business) logic — this is named as the core advantage of the product.
mandates.implication: The business-logic model is the origin point of the build, not a derivative of what source systems happen to emit. Build the DAB focal model from business concepts first; do not let source-system shape drive it.

mandates.claim: Both upstream layers (ingest) and downstream (metrics layer, BI) essentially become a function of what Daana has defined.
mandates.implication: The modeling layer is the single authoring surface. Ingest configuration and the downstream metrics/BI surface should be derived or generated from the model definition rather than hand-authored independently; hand-editing generated ingest or generated star-schema output breaks the stated architecture.

mandates.claim: To get unambiguous output from AI you must have unambiguous input; 'a dozen partially overlapping hand-crafted dbt models is not unambiguous input and any AI will struggle to make reliable output of such data.'
mandates.implication: Overlapping, redundant, hand-written model files are a defect, not a style preference. Each truth must live in exactly one place — the design should make partially-overlapping duplicate definitions impossible, not merely discouraged.

mandates.claim: The main purpose of data modeling (Kimball, Data Vault etc.) is to transform raw data into a truthful and sustainable shape that satisfies consumption; 'sustainable' is the challenging word, because it takes about a year before you see the real pains of poor or lacking modeling.
mandates.implication: Judge the consumption layer against a roughly one-year horizon, not against whether it satisfies today's query. Short-term correctness is not evidence of a good model.

mandates.claim: dbt and Medallion are named as patterns/tools that loosen modeling discipline — they basically say 'it's not that important how you write and layer your models, just make more of them, and everyone can do it.'
mandates.implication: Do not reproduce a free-form, proliferating model-file layout, nor Medallion layering as the organizing principle. The layer separation must be enforced by tooling, not by convention each engineer applies differently.

mandates.claim: The stated failure mode of undisciplined modeling after one year: 'No one knows what or where the truth lies, half of your models are redundant or orphaned, your code base has as many conventions as there are data engineers in the team.'
mandates.implication: Three explicit acceptance criteria for the platform: truth is locatable, no orphaned or redundant models can accumulate, and conventions are singular and machine-enforced rather than per-engineer.

mandates.claim: Trying to build a data stack with the same modularity (microservices etc.) as a software application makes it very hard to solve problems around single source of truth, how to process massive data sets, and teaches DEs completely new ways of working.
mandates.implication: Do not decompose the platform into independently-owned microservice-like model units. Keep the model centralized enough that single source of truth and large-scale processing remain tractable.

mandates.claim: Data Engineering should continue approaching Software Engineering, but 'it's a delicate maneuver that takes time and will be very costly if rushed'; adopting SWE practices (most things DevOps) is 'mainly great', and the naive assumption is that DE equals SWE.
mandates.implication: Adopt DevOps-style practice incrementally. Rushing full software-engineering ceremony onto the data platform is explicitly called out as a costly mistake.

mandates.claim: Data quality testing limited to 'not null' and 'is unique' is insufficient; distribution analysis can uncover a wide range of interesting data quality insights, and having an ANSI SQL starting point is very beneficial for compatibility.
mandates.implication: Plan for distribution-based/statistical checks (Kullback-Leibler divergence is the named example) in addition to null and uniqueness assertions, and express them in ANSI SQL so they remain portable across warehouse engines.

mandates.claim: The worst inherited architecture failed because the storage format was chosen without checking engine support: raw data moved to Parquet on S3-equivalent storage while the DWH had to stay on on-prem SQL Server for security reasons, and that SQL Server version did not support pruning when reading Parquet from S3, so all data had to be read on ingest.
mandates.implication: Validate that the chosen ingest storage format supports pruning on the actual query engine and version in use. A format choice the engine cannot push down into yields 'a more complex architecture with worse performance than before'.

mandates.claim: The team is 'all very invested in modern agentic workflows, which makes the product advance at incredible speed', and the current client engagement is 'building the data stack and implementing agentic workflows'.
mandates.implication: Agentic workflows are treated as part of the delivered engagement, not merely internal tooling — an implementation is expected to be built and operated with agents against the model.

quotes: Metadata-driven data modeling, starting from the actual real-world (aka business) logic, has so many advantages.
AI will automate everything, but as with any automation, to get unambiguous output you want to have unambiguous input.
A dozen partially overlapping hand-crafted dbt models is not unambiguous input and any AI will struggle to make reliable output of such data.
Both upstream layers (ingest) and downstream (metrics layer, BI) essentially become a function of what Daana has defined.
The main purpose for data modeling (Kimball, Data Vault etc.) is to transform raw data into a truthful and sustainable shape that satisfies consumption.
Add to that patterns and tools (looking at you, dbt and Medallion) that loosen the once so important discipline that rules data modeling.

A common example is trying to build a data stack with the same modularity (microservices etc.) as a software application. Doing so makes it very hard to solve problems around single source of truth, how to process massive data sets, and not to mention teaching DEs completely new ways of working.
Distribution analysis can uncover a wide range of interesting data quality insights in data, and having an ANSI SQL starting point is very beneficial for compatibility.
openQuestions: The post never names the DAS / DAB / DAR layers, dlt, daana-cli as a command, or the Unified Star Schema. Nothing here specifies how the three layers are separated, named, generated, or wired together — that must come entirely from other sources.

Which distribution/statistical tests to implement beyond null and uniqueness is explicitly left to judgment: 'Depending on use case, more sophisticated tests will pay off.' Only Kullback-Leibler divergence is given as an example, and no implementation or SQL is shown.

How far to take software-engineering practice adoption is left unresolved: DE 'should continue approaching Software Engineering, but it's a delicate maneuver that takes time and will be very costly if rushed' — no line is drawn for where modularity becomes harmful beyond the microservices example.
What makes a model 'sustainable' is named as the critical property but never operationalized; the only stated test is the passage of about a year before the real pains show up.
Whether the metrics layer and BI are literally generated from the model or merely constrained by it is ambiguous — 'essentially become a function of' is not further specified.
The Parquet/SQL Server anecdote implies engine-capability validation must precede storage-format choice, but the post gives no checklist or procedure for performing that validation.
'Implementing agentic workflows' is named as part of a typical client engagement, but no workflow, agent role, or tooling for it is described.
